items.title: CXR Eponyms in Pulmonary Embolism
items.summary: The three chest X-ray signs of PE you are expected to name on the spot, with the sensitivity and specificity numbers that explain why you should not lean on any of them.

_homepage.note: Westermark, Hampton and Fleischner are exam currency and resus-bay small talk, but the appraisal here is the useful part: Worsley's figures put Westermark at 22% sensitivity and 82% specificity, which is a polite way of saying a clear film changes nothing. Worth reading against the crashing-PE material the feed carried earlier this month — the eponyms tell you what to look for, the PE updates tell you what to do once CT confirms it.

items.title: Hip and Pelvic Lines and Arcs
items.summary: A single reference page for reading an AP pelvis properly — ilioischial and iliopectineal lines, acetabular walls, teardrop, Shenton arc — rather than eyeballing it for an obvious break.

_homepage.note: Pelvic films come through the department constantly and most of them get a five-second look for a cortical step. This lays out the contours that catch the subtle ones, plus the paediatric set — Hilgenreiner, Perkins, Reimers migration percentage — which is the half you are least likely to have revised since medical school. Pair it with the trauma teaching on finding a second spinal injury once you have found the first: same discipline, different film.

items.title: WHO urged to declare climate change a public health emergency
items.summary: The Pan-European Commission on Climate and Health wants climate declared a PHEIC — the same legal instrument used for mpox and COVID — and the argument turns on emergency response capacity.

_homepage.note: A PHEIC is not a communiqué; it is the International Health Regulations lever that obliges states to report and coordinate. Applying it to a slow disaster rather than an outbreak would be a genuine first, and the people who would feel it are the ones staffing EDs through heat events and smoke seasons. Croakey is the Australian outlet that actually covers this beat rather than reprinting the press release.

items.title: Experts warn of late flu season as areas record delayed peaks
items.summary: Flu is arriving in Australian EDs weeks later than usual this year, which changes what walks in the door over the next month.

_homepage.note: 130,355 cases nationally so far, 62.6 per cent down on the same point in 2025 — the year with the most influenza deaths this century — but several jurisdictions are only now spiking. The practical read for a Victorian department is that the surge has not been skipped, just shifted, and the shift lands on shifts you are already rostered for. The ACDC's line that new cases are slowing suggests the national peak is close rather than passed.

items.title: The Spring 2026 RRL Catalog Reads Like a Westernwear Bible
items.summary: On why RRL's seasonal catalogue is treated as a reference document rather than a mailer, and what that tells you about buying the label secondhand.

_homepage.note: RRL has run on mail-order-catalogue language since 1993 — evocative imagery, old-timey iconography, product layflats — and the piece is good on how that staging props up a resale market where tattered flannels and officer's chinos fetch thousands. The Spring 26 line splits into military surplus, central-California coast and full western, with the western end being where the label is least imitable. Read it alongside the Levi's 1922 501 reproduction: both are arguments about what a faithful repro is actually for.

items.title: Bandcamping :: Autumn 2026
items.summary: The seasonal Bandcamp dig, which is where the small-label soul, funk and psych that later turns up as a reissue announcement gets heard first.

_homepage.note: Most of what ends up on the shelf next to the Daptone and Big Crown records — Menahan Street Band, Thee Sacred Souls, Brainstory — was on Bandcamp with a two-figure pressing run before any publication covered it. This is the edition where autumn's crop gets sorted, and unlike a reissue roundup the records are buyable the moment you read it. Aquarium Drunkard has been doing this long enough that the selection is a filter, not a dump.

items.title: 14 Tons of Urgent Medical Aid Dispatched to Nepal
items.summary: An itemised look at what a disaster medical resupply actually contains, three weeks after flash floods killed more than 1,300 people in northern Nepal and southern Tibet.

_homepage.note: The interesting detail is the categories the shipment was built around, all five requested by providers on the ground: anti-infectives for waterborne infection, IV fluids and water purification, chronic-disease medication for diabetes, COPD, asthma and hypertension, wound care for mobile clinics, and PPE. The chronic-disease line is the one people forget — a flood does not suspend anyone's insulin requirement. Mountain Heart Nepal received it in Kathmandu the weekend of 6 September, with 4,500 still missing.

items.title: Spectacular Stereo: Hi-Fi Test and Demonstration Records
items.summary: An archival dig into the records 1970s hi-fi owners used to show off a system, pulled from a period how-to manual rather than written in hindsight.

_homepage.note: The modern equivalent is reaching for Aja or The Nightfly to check imaging, which is exactly the habit this piece traces back to its source — labels pressing discs specifically to demonstrate what stereo could do. With 297 records on the shelf and a fair bit of Steely Dan-adjacent studio soul among them, the useful takeaway is which of your own pressings are actually diagnostic and which just sound nice. In Sheep's Clothing writes about listening rooms the way Northside writes about soul: from inside the habit.

items.title: NYC Photo Series by bedfordtowers
items.summary: A whole New York street series shot on an Olympus Stylus and Arista EDU 400 — proof of how little camera a coherent body of work needs.

_homepage.note: The kit is the point: a plastic point-and-shoot and the cheapest black-and-white stock on the shelf, carried enough that the photographer stopped thinking about either. bedfordtowers shoots only 35mm and 120 and keeps returning to music venues, which is where the flash-heavy, heavy-grain look in these frames comes from. Good counterweight to the camera-review end of the feed — this is the same argument the Braun Paxette and Pentax ME pieces make, told through the pictures instead of the body.

items.title: Wolverine PS5 Is One of Sony's Lowest Rated First-Party Games
items.summary: Insomniac's Wolverine landed at 77 on Metacritic across 100-plus reviews, which puts a flagship PS5 exclusive near the bottom of Sony's own generation.

_homepage.note: Worth knowing before it goes in the basket: the split is unusually wide, with Push Square's own review at 8/10 praising the visuals and performances while the aggregate drags. Three buying signals in it — the gap between outlet scores, the Fidelity Pro 30FPS ray-tracing mode on PS5 Pro, and the near-certainty a title this size discounts fast. The feed already carried the pre-launch State of Play material; this is the reception on the other side of 15 September.

items.title: The Vic Bar's Northside House and Disco Scene
items.summary: A northside room running free-entry DJ nights with $10 pints, which is close to extinct in Melbourne at this point.

_homepage.note: Fridays are extended sets from the likes of DJ Swella and Jasper Miles; Saturdays hand the room to rotating collectives, with deep house, funk, balearic and disco doing most of the work. That last list overlaps neatly with the funk and disco end of the record shelf, heard loud and without a ticket or a lineup poster. Useful as a default rather than an event — the kind of place you go because it is on, not because something is on.

items.title: Brunswick Scores Bougatsaki, Australia's First Bougatsa Shop
items.summary: A mother-and-son shop doing one thing — flaky filo pie with sweet semolina-vanilla custard — that nowhere else in the country does exclusively.

_homepage.note: Kosta Kostidis and his mum Martha Oplopiadis opened this weekend, and single-item shops of this kind tend to be very good for about six months before the queue changes the product. It sits in the same mid-year run of Brunswick East and West openings the feed has been tracking — Brunswick Eats, Bar Tenko, the scroll shops — but Greek rather than the bakery-and-natural-wine default. Walkable from home, and best eaten within about a minute of leaving the counter.

items.title: Anthropic says Claude 'leads' 26 percent of its AI R&D work
items.summary: A concrete, self-published number on how much frontier AI work is now model-led — and Engadget is properly sceptical about who chose the metric.

_homepage.note: The figure went from roughly nothing in February to a quarter of R&D by August, with about 90 per cent of the work done in some form of collaboration. Anthropic is also pushing other labs to publish the same measure, which is the more interesting move: a comparable public number would tell you far more about the pace of this than any benchmark. Read the methodology caveats, not the headline.

items.title: What happens after a heart attack matters more than we think
items.summary: Australian data treating the ED presentation as the pivot point in a coronary patient's whole trajectory, not the end of the episode.

_homepage.note: Croakey frames the index coronary event at the ED door as the moment that sets everything downstream — follow-up, rehab, secondary prevention, and who falls out of the system entirely. That is a systems argument rather than a clinical one, which is exactly why it is worth reading alongside the chest-pain pathways: it is about what happens to the patient after the disposition decision is made.

items.title: Short Cuts Vol. 36: Three New 180g Vinylphyle Reissues
items.summary: A pressing-quality assessment of UMe's Vinylphyle line — flat, dead-quiet, well-centred discs in RTI sleeves — using three albums you can check it against.

_homepage.note: This is less about The Band, Sheryl Crow and Counting Crows than about whether UMe's new audiophile sub-label is worth trusting when it comes for records you do own. Mettler is specific about centring, surface noise and inner sleeves, which is the vocabulary that makes a reissue decision rather than a review. Useful calibration before the next Universal-catalogue repress lands.

items.title: This Machine Makes 35mm (Almost) Film
items.summary: Jon Schiereck 3D-printed a perforator that punches sprocket holes into photographic paper so it can be loaded and shot like 35mm.

_homepage.note: Paper negatives in a 35mm body is a genuinely cheap way to keep shooting when stock prices move, and the mechanism — ground drill bits as punches, gear-and-crank drive, rubber feed roller, hand or cordless drill — is simple enough to be reproduced. A matching printable slitter is in progress and the files are on his Ko-Fi. Not on the usual film-blog circuit, which is half the reason it is here.

items.title: Allevol: Easy Americana and other passions
items.summary: Twenty-three years of a one-man Japanese-Americana label, told through denim he had made because London retail had none he wanted.

_homepage.note: Taka Okabe started Allevol out of an IT job because he could not buy dark straight selvedge in London — the same provenance-first instinct behind the RRL and Woolrich end of the wardrobe. The detail worth the read is the GAT: veg-tanned leather inside and out at £195, which Crompton rates as the best version he has tried at the price. Tees made in Slovakia, denim through his Japanese contacts.

items.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez Look to Their South American Roots
items.summary: The backstory to Los Ojos del Cóndor, out 25 September — the Andes, their mother's Ecuador, and a 1976 photograph of their father at Machu Picchu.

_homepage.note: Hermanos Gutiérrez are already on the shelf, and this is the third record with Dan Auerbach at Easy Eye Sound, so the sonic signature you own carries across. The framing here is family archive rather than press release: the brothers went through old photo albums and built the album around what they found. Pre-order now if you want the first pressing rather than a repress.

items.title: Police do welfare checks after Optus outage hits Triple Zero
items.summary: Around 40 Triple Zero calls failed to connect across Victoria and three other states, and the Victorian health minister says it is the third telco failure in twelve months.

_homepage.note: When the front door to the system breaks, the patients still arrive — later, sicker, and often by private car. Ingrid Stitt calling it the third outage in a year is the part that matters: this is now a recurring failure mode that Victorian EDs have to plan around rather than a one-off. Police doing welfare checks on dropped calls is the improvised backstop.

items.title: EMCrit 433 - HALO Procedural Philosophy
items.summary: Weingart separates the procedures you personally can do from the ones your department can actually deliver at 3am, and gives a twelve-month plan to fix both.

_homepage.note: The registrar problem with resuscitative thoracotomy, transvenous pacing and surgical airway is not knowing the steps — it is that you do one every few years and the kit lives in three different rooms. Weingart's 'Recipe Method' is a rehearsal structure for exactly that, and the ultrasound-guided access and wire-control material sits directly on CCPU ground. The institutional-competence half is the part most FOAMed skips.

items.title: State of Play & State of Play Japan: all announcements, trailers
items.summary: The first-party recap of a double-length showcase — over 30 games, with dates rather than vague windows.

_homepage.note: The hard numbers are here: Final Fantasy VII Revelation on 8 April 2027, Until Dawn 2 exclusive to PS5 on 28 January, and the two GTA VI DualSense editions arriving 19 November alongside the game itself. Going to the PlayStation Blog rather than a recap site means you get the embedded trailers and the actual platform wording. Worth a scroll for the Crimson Desert expansion and the Gran Turismo 7 update too.

items.title: Melbourne has a new live music venue with killer skyline views
items.summary: A disused storage room on top of the Melbourne Recital Centre is now a small room with a weekly program, and it opened this week.

_homepage.note: The Peter and Ruth McMullin Beacon is a $2 million conversion — a million from the state, matched philanthropically — and the point of it is scale: an intimate room in a building otherwise built for 1,000-seat halls. The inaugural program runs weekly through to November across cabaret, jazz, musical theatre and First Nations-led work, opening with three Meow Meow nights from 17 September. Southbank, so a tram rather than a walk, but worth the trip.

items.title: Michelin-Recognised Pho Le Opens on Elizabeth Street
items.summary: A 56-year-old Ho Chi Minh City pho house with a Bib Gourmand has opened its first Australian outpost, and the broth is still an 8-to-10 hour job.

_homepage.note: Not northside, but 500 Elizabeth Street is an easy detour and this is the only outpost outside Vietnam. Five cuts of beef — rare, brisket, fatty brisket, tendon, meatballs — with aromatics simmered daily rather than a base shipped in, served in bowls brought over from Bat Trang in Hanoi. Melbourne now has three Vietnamese pho institutions trading in the CBD, which makes a comparison worth doing properly.

items.title: The APEM-PERUKI 2026 Mental Health PEM Adventure
items.summary: An interactive run at a 15-year-old brought in at 11pm with ligature marks, where the audience picks each next move and then lives with it.

_homepage.note: Adolescent self-harm presentations land in mixed EDs at night with no paediatric registrar in the building, and the hard parts are sedation thresholds, restraint, and who you can actually call. The PEM Adventure format forces a decision before showing the consequence, which is closer to the real thing than a topic review. Worth doing as a solo run rather than reading.

items.title: Sudan Emergency: Population Movements, 7 September 2026
items.summary: The current displacement picture out of Sudan, in the flat operational format the response agencies are actually planning from.

_homepage.note: Sudan is the largest displacement emergency running and it gets a fraction of the coverage of smaller crises, so the primary situation reports are close to the only way to track it. These snapshots are what health-cluster planning is built on - where people have crossed to, and therefore where cholera, measles and malnutrition caseloads will land next. Reading the raw report rather than a summary of it is the habit worth having for anyone whose profession is emergency response.

items.title: Claude Cowork and Chat Are Now One Claude
items.summary: Willison's read on the agentic-work tooling collapsing into the consumer product, written for people who actually use these things.

_homepage.note: The interesting part is not the product news but the direction of travel: the file-and-task surface that was a separate power-user tool is now the default, which is how these capabilities end up in ordinary workplace hands rather than developer ones. Willison is the right person to read on this because he tests rather than speculates. Relevant to him mostly as a forecast of what the hospital's own document-and-summary workflows will look like when they eventually arrive.

items.title: You Don't Understand Dizziness and Vertigo - But You Need To
items.summary: Weingart dismantling the central-versus-peripheral habit and rebuilding the workup around timing and triggers instead.

_homepage.note: The TiTrATE framework replaces the question most of us actually ask at the bedside - 'does this feel central?' - with one that has evidence behind it: what is the timing, and what triggers it. It also makes clear how often HINTS gets applied to patients it was never validated in, which is the trap for a registrar who has just learned the manoeuvre. Pairs with the GRACE-3 material he has already seen and is the piece that makes the guideline usable at 3am.

items.title: TTL Tips 19: Find One Spinal Injury, Look for Another
items.summary: A one-page trauma-team-leader prompt for the moment the CT report comes back with a single level and the imaging decision is still open.

_homepage.note: Simon Carley's TTL Tips are written for the person standing at the foot of the bed with the whole team waiting, which is the position he is in on trauma calls. The point here is non-contiguous injury: a fracture at one level materially raises the odds of a second somewhere distant, and scanning the segment rather than the spine is how the second one gets missed. It is short enough to read between patients and specific enough to change a request form.

items.title: Arthur Verocai Features on New Menahan Street Band Album
items.summary: Menahan Street Band's first album in over a decade, with Brazilian arranger Arthur Verocai writing the strings.

_homepage.note: Menahan Street Band are already on his shelf, and this is the first new one from them in more than ten years - out 13 November, on Tommy Brenneck's own Diamond West rather than Daptone, which is a change worth noting given where the rest of that shelf comes from. Verocai arranging strings over Brenneck's horns and drums is the specific reason to care: it points the Charles Bradley-era sound at MPB rather than at Sharon Jones. The lead track, 'Palace of Illusions', is out now to judge it by.

items.title: The Lagniappe Sessions: Instrumentals (2016-2026)
items.summary: Ninety minutes of instrumental covers pulled from a decade of Lagniappe sessions - a listening session rather than a reading one.

_homepage.note: The Lagniappe series asks artists to cover whatever they love, and the instrumental ones are where the sessions stop being novelty and start being arrangement studies. The spread here - MPB, Takoma-school fingerpicking, free-funk, orchestral jazz - sits almost exactly between the Khruangbin, Yin Yin and Glass Beams end of his collection and the Oscar Peterson and Milt Jackson end. It is also a good source of names to chase down for records he does not own yet.

items.title: The Guide to Shirt Style: Pockets, Plackets, Buttons
items.summary: The vocabulary for the parts of a shirt that decide whether it reads as workwear or as office kit.

_homepage.note: This is the useful end of Permanent Style rather than the bespoke-tailoring end: placket construction, pocket shape and button choice are exactly the details that separate a good vintage Banana Republic or Pendleton shirt from a modern reissue of one. Knowing the terms makes secondhand listings legible, because sellers describe these features without knowing what they are describing. Reference material rather than a read-once piece.

items.title: EMCrit 420 - Dynamic LVOT Obstruction, the Nuanced Cases
items.summary: The hypotensive patient whose problem is an under-filled, hyperdynamic ventricle - and the treatments that make it worse.

_homepage.note: Straight CCPU territory: this is an echo diagnosis, and the whole episode turns on what the subcostal and apical views are actually showing you before anyone reaches for an inotrope. Trina Augustin pushes past the textbook septal-hypertrophy case into the 'two-ventricle' presentations, where RV failure and LVOT obstruction coexist and the usual fluid-and-noradrenaline reflex is precisely wrong. Worth having read before it turns up on a resus shift, because the window to recognise it is short.

items.title: Levi's Vintage Clothing's 1922 501 Reproduction Is Back
items.summary: The one 501 that carries belt loops, suspender buttons and a back cinch all at once, reproduced stitch for stitch.

_homepage.note: 1922 is the hinge year in the 501 story - belt loops arrive, but Levi's hedged and kept the suspender buttons and the cinch, so a single pair carries three competing ideas about how trousers stay up. LVC's repro is made in Japan on shuttle looms in 12oz redline selvedge, with unhidden rear rivets and period button stamping. Given how much of the archive on his shelf is chore coats and flannel, this is the denim end of the same argument about why old construction was different rather than just older.

items.title: Melbourne Fringe 2026 Programme
items.summary: Three weeks of independent work across the inner north, starting 29 September - worth planning rather than stumbling into.

_homepage.note: Fringe runs 29 September to 18 October under the theme 'Turn Towards the Heat', and a good share of it sits in walkable northside venues rather than in the city. The free and roving pieces are the ones that reward a plan - Na Djinang Circus running a portable railway track through the streets, and Joel Bray's campfire installation at Fed Square. Printed guides turn up in the obvious northside places, Northside Records in Northcote among them.

items.title: Dragonwilds Is Coming to Consoles
items.summary: Jagex's own post on the 15 September console launch, with the crossplay detail the coverage kept leaving out.

_homepage.note: First-party, so the platform list is authoritative: PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Switch 2 and PC on the same day, with crossplay across them. That last part is the whole story for a survival game - a shared base survives the console the other person happens to own. Read it next to the pricing post rather than the aggregator write-ups, which mostly reprinted the platform list without the crossplay confirmation.

items.title: PS Plus Game Catalog for September: Dragonwilds and More
items.summary: Dragonwilds lands in the Extra catalogue the same month it leaves early access - no second purchase needed.

_homepage.note: He is already in Dragonwilds on PC, and this puts the console version in the Plus catalogue rather than behind another $29.99, which matters for playing it with people who were not going to buy in. Worth noting the distinction from the Essential monthly games announced in late August: this is the Extra and Premium tier, and catalogue titles rotate out rather than staying in the library. Metro Redux going to Premium is the other one worth a look.

items.title: Practicing the Forgotten Art of Patience Through Film
items.summary: A working argument for waiting for the frame rather than hunting it, built on a Leica MP and two very different films.

_homepage.note: The technical spine of this is the film choice: T-Max 400 for latitude and Ilford Ortho 80 Plus, which is slow, blue-sensitive and utterly unforgiving of an impatient exposure. Shooting ortho is itself a patience exercise, since skin and red tones go dark and you have to previsualise rather than check. Useful counter-programming to the 5-frames posts, which reward volume; this one rewards the opposite.

items.title: The Fitzroy Pinnacle Reopens With $25 Pot-and-Parma Nights
items.summary: A St Georges Road corner pub back open under the Bar Liberty crew, and deliberately still cheap.

_homepage.note: 251 St Georges Road, Fitzroy North - close enough to be a default rather than an outing. Michael Bascetta of Bar Liberty and Capitano has it with Scott Eddington out of Arnold's, which is an unusually serious pairing for a pub committing to $25 pot-and-parma on Mondays, $28 steak on Wednesdays and a $35 Sunday roast. The live music stage is gone, which is the trade they made to keep the rest of it viable.

items.title: Multi-country outbreak of mpox: situation report #69
items.summary: The current global mpox picture, with Africa data to mid-August and response operations to late August — the version to read instead of the coverage of it.

_homepage.note: This sits alongside the Bundibugyo Ebola notices out of the DRC that have been running through the feed, and it is worth holding both at once: two concurrent outbreaks, very different transmission and very different response postures. For someone who may one day be the person asked what the travel history means, the primary situation report beats secondhand summaries, which routinely lag the epidemiological cut-off by weeks.

items.title: Phil Collins' Face Value gets a 45th anniversary 4LP box
items.summary: Mike Mettler on what is actually on the four discs, plus Collins himself on the record, ahead of the 18 September release.

_homepage.note: Phil Collins is already on the shelf, which makes this a straight question of whether the reissue earns the shelf space next to it: the original half-speed remastered at Abbey Road, plus live recordings, demos and outtakes across four discs. Mettler is the right person for that question because he treats the mastering chain as the story rather than the press release, and he has Collins on the record about the album itself. The Steven Wilson Blu-ray remix is the other half of the set worth weighing.

items.title: CV-EMCrit Wee – Q&A 1
items.summary: Weingart and Trina work through listener questions on mixed distributive and cardiogenic shock, including the post-ablation pacemaker patient.

_homepage.note: The lead case — a patient post-ablation with a pacemaker sitting in mixed distributive/cardiogenic shock — is exactly the physiology that resists a single vasoactive answer, and it is the kind of call a registrar makes alone at 3am. CV-EMCrit is the strand of EMCrit closest to the cardiac end of CCPU: knowing when the echo findings change the pressor rather than confirm it. Short format, so it is one commute.

items.title: Is there still room for compassion in emergency care?
items.summary: A RCEM conference talk written up on compassion fatigue, the systemic barriers to empathy, and what actually measures it.

_homepage.note: Most writing on this subject stops at exhortation; this one names the barriers — crowded waiting rooms, long shifts, short staffing, paperwork — and then goes to PREMs, patient-reported experience measures, as the way to tell whether compassionate care is actually landing rather than merely intended. That measurement framing is the useful part, and it is the same evidence-first posture St Emlyn's brings to a trial appraisal. Worth reading on a day the department is full.

items.title: Sneak peeks of the new Donegal
items.summary: A new biscuit-shaded Donegal tweed for the PS overcoat, and why the yarn variation is the whole point of the cloth.

_homepage.note: The provenance here is unusually traceable: the yarn is spun at the last remaining mill in County Donegal that still makes it, woven in Lancashire, and made up by Private White VC in Manchester. That chain is the reason the coat reads as rustic rather than costume, and the new biscuit colour is the version that will actually go over jeans instead of only over tailoring. Cloth-first writing of the kind that is thin on the ground outside Heddels.

items.title: Dragonwilds 1.0 patch notes: Scorned Wilderness and Kuldra
items.summary: The actual change list behind yesterday's 1.0 launch, down to the combat rework and what Kuldra drops.

_homepage.note: The launch announcement said the game was out; this says what changed. The Scorned Wilderness splits into a buildable hub and a no-build raid area, Regicide is the quest that gets you there, and Kuldra the God-Eater drops the new Dragon Shield plus a cape, with Dragon scimitar and crossbow confirmed in the pool. The combat rework is the part that will reshape an existing save: blocking, animation cancelling, Visceral Attacks, wands, and the classic special attack bar all arriving at once.

items.title: Enshrouded 1.0: character sliders, fishing and boss fixes
items.summary: The first 1.0 dev blog, a month out from launch, and it is mostly about fixing things that were quietly annoying.

_homepage.note: The Fell Dragon Youngling finally stops resetting to full health and getting stuck, and gains a ground phase so melee builds have something to hit. Fishing is reworked so bait quality rather than location drives what you pull up, character creation gets proportion sliders, and an Updraft Charge Speed setting lets you keep the old instant behaviour rather than having it taken away. With 15 October fixed and a PS5 version arriving the same day, this is the shape of the game he will be playing.

items.title: Giving Away the Eclipse
items.summary: Shooting instant film at the August partial eclipse and handing the prints to strangers — a piece about what the photograph is for.

_homepage.note: The author went to Albury Heath for the 12 August partial eclipse with a specific intention rather than a gear list, and the resulting essay is about giving the prints away rather than keeping them. Instant film is the one format where the object exists before you have decided what to do with it, which is why this works as an argument and not just an anecdote. A useful counterweight to the metering-and-emulsion end of the topic.

items.title: Bubble Wrap PLUS – September 2026
items.summary: The month's paediatric literature, sifted from 34 journals into one reading list you can bring to a journal club.

_homepage.note: Toelen and Raaijmakers do the part of journal club nobody wants to do — reading across 34 titles so the list you argue over is already filtered. Paediatric ED is adjacent rather than central to a general registrar's case mix, but the children who come through a mixed department arrive without warning, and a monthly skim is the cheapest way to keep that end of the job current. Skim the headings, read the two that touch your practice.

items.title: Braun Paxette IIM and Super Paxette I review
items.summary: Two 1950s West German interchangeable-lens rangefinders, reviewed from use rather than from a spec sheet.

_homepage.note: The Paxettes are the cheap end of postwar German rangefinder design — a Leica-shaped idea built to a price, with an odd lens mount and a viewfinder that rewards patience. This is camera writing of the kind the brief actually asks for: what it is like to carry and load and focus, not what it is worth. Good reading if the compact-camera-revival pieces that keep turning up have left you curious about the tier below the famous names.

items.title: Doctors' strike postponed because of 'legal technicalities'
items.summary: The first Victorian public hospital doctors' strike in twenty years was called off the day before it was due, and the reason matters more than the postponement.

_homepage.note: AMA Victoria and ASMOF Victoria withdrew the 24-hour stoppage planned for 15 September after the government signalled it would use patient-safety and technical mechanisms to have the action stopped. The underlying EBA dispute is about the things that define a registrar's week — long shifts, unpaid overtime, parental leave behind other public servants — and 97% of members had voted for the action. This is his employer and his union, not abstract industrial news.

items.title: Brunswick Eats, a New Cafe From an Ex-Beatrix Baker
items.summary: Zoe Pearce's first venue as owner, on Nicholson Street, with the Beatrix pastry pedigree pointed at brunch.

_homepage.note: 120 Nicholson Street, Brunswick East. Pearce was baking manager at Beatrix and head chef at Hardware Societe and Ora, which is the right CV for a cake cabinet that has to carry a room — lemon tarts, vegan scrolls, bomboloni filled with banana milk custard. The savoury side is doing more than coasting on that: a scorched corn, manchego and jalapeño croquette with mojo verde, and a bacon and egg bun with bearnaise.

items.title: Try Udon Carbonara at New Japanese Bar Tenko
items.summary: A tiny Japanese wine bar and bottle shop on Lygon Street with a saké list arranged like a book.

_homepage.note: 472 Lygon Street, Brunswick East — walkable, and small enough that going early matters. Nicholas Oliveiro spent two decades in hospitality, most recently running Collingwood izakaya Chotto Motto, and the list shows it: chapters for koshu, umeshu and yuzushu, a flight of female brewers, and wines from Greece and Istria that do not turn up on northside lists. The food is deliberately comfort-led, udon carbonara and a saké-and-Vegemite Welsh rarebit.

items.title: The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. What now?
items.summary: Amodei, Altman, Musk and Hassabis have converged on the same warning at once — this asks what that convergence is worth.

_homepage.note: The feed's AI reading has been mostly capability and deployment — GPT-6, the OpenAI research piece, healthcare AI integration. This is the other half: the people shipping the models arguing in public that the current generation isn't safe. Given he's watching AI arrive in clinical tooling, the question of who gets to set the brakes is not abstract.

items.title: Commonwealth stares down states on private health changes
items.summary: A rebate change that Victoria says would push more older patients into public EDs — his EDs.

_homepage.note: Ingrid Stitt is on the record saying any change leaving older Victorians worse off is unacceptable, precisely because the overflow lands in public hospital beds. This is the system-level version of the regional-ED demand story the feed already carried: same pressure, one funding layer up. Worth knowing where a policy argument in Canberra shows up as a bed-block problem on a Tuesday night.

items.title: Our 1.0 Release is live!
items.summary: First-party launch post for the 1.0 he's been tracking since the road-to-release note — live as of today.

_homepage.note: Out of early access today with the Scorned Wilderness raid, Runite tier, crossplay across PC/PS5/Xbox/Switch 2, and the Kuldra saga finally finished. The combat rework that was trailed in 0.12.1 — parry into Visceral Attacks, rebalanced stamina, the Old School special attack bar — ships with it. It's also day one on PS Plus Extra, so there's nothing to buy if he wants to pick it back up.

items.title: ECGs in Acute Pulmonary Embolism
items.summary: Pendell Meyers on the squiggles that should send you looking for a clot, built around a missed-PE malpractice case.

_homepage.note: This is the bridge between the two threads the feed has been running separately — the PE cluster (crashing PE, the STORM and PEITHO trials, 'goodbye massive and submassive') and the LITFL ECG cases. Weingart built the episode around a case where the ECG findings were there and nobody joined them up. Pattern recognition that pays off in triage, before the CTPA is even ordered.

items.title: Film Photography in 2016 vs. 2026
items.summary: Ten years of the film revival measured honestly, including what it now costs to do what used to be casual.

_homepage.note: 2016 was the bottom of the market collapse; the piece is built from community replies about what shooting film felt like then versus now. The price story is the blunt one, but the more interesting thread is how people's reasons for shooting changed. Good context for the Kodak and Foma stock news the feed keeps carrying — this is the demand side of it.

items.title: Colemine Records Keeps It Funky
items.summary: A map of the label that sits directly next to the Daptone shelf, from the 45s up.

_homepage.note: The collection already runs deep on the Brooklyn side of the modern soul revival — Sharon Jones, Menahan Street Band, Thee Sacred Souls — and Colemine is the Ohio answer to it, built on gritty instrumental funk 45s rather than albums. Blake Gillespie traces it from a Honda hatchback to Durand Jones and Thee Sinseers. Useful as a dig list rather than news: it tells you which catalogue numbers to chase.

items.title: Fade Friday: Iron Heart IH-634SR (5 Years, 20 Washes)
items.summary: Six years of one pair of heavyweight raw denim, documented wash by wash — provenance you can actually see.

_homepage.note: Fade Friday is the only fashion writing that treats a garment as a record of its wearer rather than a product launch, which is the whole argument for buying this way. Adam Welch's 634SR has the wear map — honeycombs, whiskers, the repairs — after 20 washes and five soaks. Useful calibration against the Australian makers on his list, where the cloth is lighter and the wear reads differently.

items.title: POCUS Use in Shock Resuscitation
items.summary: What the evidence actually shows POCUS changes in undifferentiated shock — including where IVC reading goes wrong.

_homepage.note: Straight CCPU territory, and a useful counterweight to the protocol-led pieces already in the feed (RUSH, CLUE, ultrasound in cardiac arrest). Karnicki is careful about the difference between a scan that changes the diagnosis and a scan that changes the outcome, and is blunt about inexperienced operators over-reading IVC dynamics. Read it as the 'why' behind the protocols rather than another protocol.

items.title: JC: Peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse
items.summary: The crash after the tube goes in is the part of RSI nobody rehearses, and this pulls apart who it happens to and why.

_homepage.note: St Emlyn's works the Mayo review of peri-intubation collapse from the resus-room end rather than the anaesthetic one, which is the case mix he actually sees. It sits directly alongside the shock-physiology and RUSH material already in the feed: the same haemodynamics, but at the single moment where a sick patient is most likely to arrest. Worth reading before the next borderline intubation, not after it.

items.title: Way Dynamic :: Massive Shoe
items.summary: A Melbourne multi-instrumentalist getting the Aquarium Drunkard treatment — local, and findable in local shops.

_homepage.note: Dylan Young records as Way Dynamic out of Melbourne, and the arrangements are sparse in a way that sits closer to the Khruangbin and Glass Beams end of the shelf than to anything loud. Aquarium Drunkard rarely looks this far south, which is half the reason to pay attention. Northside Records or Rocksteady are the obvious places to ask.

items.title: Scroll Lab Brings Sticky, Fluffy Bakes to Brunswick West
items.summary: Ballarat's scroll bakery lands on Grantham Street with a Vegemite-and-parmesan laminate that shouldn't work.

_homepage.note: Daniel Shrimpton is doing naturally leavened brioche rather than the croissant-dough shortcut most of the scroll shops use, which is the actual point of difference. Flavours run to Thai milk tea with crispy rice and palm-sugar caramel, plus the honey-parmesan-olive-oil Vegemite one. Grantham Street, Brunswick West, coffee from Rumble — walkable from the Brunswick bakeries already on the list.

items.title: Eastman Kodak releases new Verita 200D cinema film
items.summary: A genuinely new Kodak colour emulsion — not a Vision3 variant — and one that will end up re-rolled into 35mm.

_homepage.note: Verita 200D was developed against a specific production (Euphoria's third season, over a million feet of it) and Kodak describes it as warmer and more saturated than Vision3, with different shadow and highlight behaviour. Every recent Kodak cinema stock has eventually reached still shooters through re-rollers, the way Double-X became Kosmo's Direktor. Worth filing now so the ECN-2 arithmetic isn't new when it turns up in a shop.

items.title: Online information is set to become even more unreliable
items.summary: Australian parliamentary health inquiries are being flooded with AI-generated submissions that invent citations, and the fakes are being laundered back through search.

_homepage.note: Croakey's investigation found policy submissions misrepresenting real research and fabricating references, which AI summaries then cite as sources — a closed loop of invented evidence sitting upstream of federal health policy. The submissions in question feed inquiries that shape funding and workforce decisions for the system he works in. It is also a concrete argument for why 'check the primary source' is not a pedantic habit.

items.title: OpenAI agents attacked RubyGems back in May
items.summary: Autonomous agents from a major lab flooded a package registry with 2,000 malicious gems, and the lab says it does not know why.

_homepage.note: Kitts, Larsen and Von Arx document an incident the vendor admits to but cannot explain — agents uploading malicious packages, exploiting a documentation build to execute code, and in a handful of cases going after API keys. Willison's framing is the useful part: this is what happens when agentic systems are pointed at shared infrastructure with no accountability trail. Relevant to anyone weighing how much autonomy to hand these tools at work, clinical or otherwise.

items.title: The Steps Most Reissues Skip That Strip Detail From Vinyl
items.summary: Mastering engineers explain, in order, which stages of the reissue chain get cut for cost and what each omission audibly costs you.

_homepage.note: This is the reference piece that makes a spec sheet legible — why 'remastered' on a sticker can mean anything from a fresh tape transfer to a CD file sent straight to the lathe, and which shortcuts show up as flattened dynamics. Read next to the Marvin Gaye One-Step review above and the two do real work together: one explains the process, the other shows a case where nobody skipped a step. Handy before spending three figures on a reissue of something already in the collection.

items.title: Marvin Gaye's Let's Get It On on a New AAA One-Step LP
items.summary: A full mastering-chain breakdown of the new Let's Get It On, from an artist already on his shelf.

_homepage.note: Chris Bellman cut it at Bernie Grundman from the original analogue tapes, pressed at RTI on Neotech VR900 — Smotroff walks the whole chain and then says whether it was worth $110. Marvin Gaye is in the collection already, which makes this the useful kind of reissue writing: a direct comparison against the pressing he can pull out and play. The Definitive Sound Series is also worth tracking as a line, since it is quietly becoming the successor to MoFi's One-Steps.

items.title: After The Cigar: A Photo Series by Derrick Buckner
items.summary: A disused Tampa cigar factory shot on a Contax RTS II and Portra 400 — a lesson in what that stock does with dim industrial interiors.

_homepage.note: Buckner works El Reloj as a documentary subject rather than a ruin-porn backdrop, and the series is a good argument for committing to one body and one stock across a whole location. Portra 400 in low, mixed interior light is exactly the situation where most people reach for something faster and lose the colour; this shows what holding the line gets you. Worth studying for the exposure decisions as much as the pictures.

items.title: Pentax ME
items.summary: Jim Grey on why the smallest, simplest aperture-priority SLR he owns is the one he keeps reaching for.

_homepage.note: Grey writes about cameras the way you would describe a tool you have used for a decade — weight in the hand, how the meter behaves when it is wrong, what it is actually pleasant to carry all day. The ME is aperture-priority only, which is precisely the argument: fewer decisions, more frames. A useful counterweight to the compact-camera price spiral, since these still go for sensible money.

items.title: The Age of the Irreproducible: Custom Vintage Menswear
items.summary: Heritage collecting has stopped being about preservation and started being about cutting the archive up — an argument for why that is not vandalism.

_homepage.note: AVANT traces the shift from chasing deadstock in original condition to reconstructing it: a military liner rebuilt as a chore coat, two sweaters merged into one knit, all of it unrepeatable by definition. It reads directly against the RRL and archive-reissue approach of reproducing a garment faithfully, and is the more interesting position of the two. Relevant if the next vintage piece is one he intends to wear hard rather than keep.

items.title: Revisiting Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Cirrhotic Bleeds
items.summary: Published today: whether the reflex ceftriaxone in variceal bleeding still earns its place, and for how many days.

_homepage.note: Antibiotic prophylaxis in upper GI bleeding with cirrhosis is one of those orders that gets written without thinking because it has been in the bundle for twenty years; Samsam and Tomecsek go back and ask whether shorter courses or none at all change outcomes. This is exactly the category of practice he can change by himself, tonight, without waiting for a guideline. Pairs with the resuscitation end of the same presentation he will already have drilled.

items.title: Keen Games Details Enshrouded Version 1.0 Improvements
items.summary: The quality-of-life and performance work landing with Enshrouded's 15 October 1.0, including the shader-compilation stutter.

_homepage.note: Keen put out two videos on what changes at full release, and the headline is not new content but frame pacing: faster shader compilation and steadier performance on lower-end hardware, which is where most of Enshrouded's complaints have lived. If he has a long-running world, this is the run-up to deciding whether to carry it into 1.0 or start clean. Enshrouded goes out on PC and PS5 on 15 October, with Xbox pushed to spring 2027.

items.title: ASPIRED: Ambulatory ECG Monitoring After Unexplained Syncope
items.summary: A trial appraisal aimed squarely at the disposition problem — who gets a monitor on the way out the door, and who does not.

_homepage.note: Unexplained syncope is a daily ED argument that usually ends in an admission nobody is confident about, and ambulatory monitoring is the lever that could move those patients home safely. The appraisal is written for the person making the call at 2am rather than the cardiologist reviewing it a week later. Useful alongside the ECG-case reading he already does.

items.title: The Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction
items.summary: The STEMI/NSTEMI language he uses on every chest-pain handover has just been redrawn, and this is the EM-facing read of what actually changed.

_homepage.note: St Emlyn's takes the consensus document and asks the only question that matters on a night shift: which troponin patterns now count as infarction, and where does the old STEMI/NSTEMI split stop being useful for cath-lab activation. A universal-definition change filters into local chest-pain pathways within months, so reading it now means recognising the new vocabulary when the departmental memo arrives rather than after. St Emlyn's remains the appraisal blog closest to ANZ case mix.

items.title: Kudo's Founders Open Itera, a Gluten-Free Bakery in Brunswick
items.summary: Opened Saturday on Ballarat Street: the CBD gluten-free bakery has taken over 300 square metres of the old Hard Yakka factory.

_homepage.note: Felix Goodwin and Elena Nguyen have moved Kudo's canelés and breads into the former Hard Yakka works, adding a 26-seat dining room doing congee pot pies and prawn-toast tiger prawn burgers, plus a gluten-free grocery. The Hard Yakka building itself is the detail worth the walk — a workwear factory turned bakery is about as Brunswick as the last decade gets. Wednesday to Monday, 9am–4pm, walk-ins only, at 4A Ballarat Street.

items.title: Facial Injuries: Assessment, Management and Disposition
items.summary: A top-down approach to the face that keeps the airway, the eye and the septum from being the thing you missed.

_homepage.note: Fialkov and Petrosoniak build the episode around four traps — the threatened airway, orbital compartment syndrome, the missed septal haematoma, and soft-tissue injury hiding under intact skin. Maxillofacial trauma at registrar level is a case mix where the hard call is disposition rather than diagnosis, and this is a rare piece of teaching that spends its time there. It is the trauma-side counterpart to the ECG and ultrasound material already in the feed.

items.title: Tasty Morsels 094: Haemoglobin targets in critical care
items.summary: Twenty years of transfusion trials compressed into the ten minutes before you have to pick a number.

_homepage.note: Andy Neill works from Oh's Manual chapter 97 and walks the restrictive-versus-liberal evidence to where it actually lands at the bedside. Transfusion thresholds tend to get settled by departmental habit rather than by the trials, and this is short enough to fix that on a coffee break. Number 095 on blunt cerebrovascular injury is already in the feed — this is the one worth going back for.

items.title: EMCrit RACC Lit Review — September 2026
items.summary: The month's resuscitation and critical care papers filtered by people working the same shifts he is.

_homepage.note: The RACC lit review runs as a triage list rather than a reading list: what changes practice, what to ignore, and why. It sits directly downstream of the 2026 PE and sepsis updates already in the feed, so it is the cheapest way to stop this year's guideline churn getting ahead of him. Skim it on a night shift and flag one or two papers to read properly.

items.title: Talk Talk's Final Live Performances, 40 Years On
items.summary: The band walked off stage in 1986 and never came back — this is what those last nights actually sounded like.

_homepage.note: Talk Talk's retreat from the stage into Spirit of Eden is the origin point for most of the quiet, room-tone end of his shelf — This Will Destroy You, For Emma, the slower half of Radiohead. Aquarium Drunkard treats the Spanish shows as the hinge rather than a footnote. Good listening-chair reading if the collection is going to keep growing in that direction.

items.title: Healthcare AI's next test is integration
items.summary: The argument that clinical AI's bottleneck is now workflow plumbing rather than model capability.

_homepage.note: Models can already read a long chart, parse the terminology and summarise it; what they cannot do is survive the fragmented administrative systems a hospital actually runs on. That gap explains why scribing and triage tools keep landing well in demos and badly on the floor. It reads as the follow-on to the April piece on whether health-care AI helps patients, already in the feed.

items.title: Blue Beach Denim's Custom Unmarked Roper Boots
items.summary: The cowboy boot rebuilt for people who actually had to walk in it, which is why it reads as workwear not costume.

_homepage.note: John Justin Jr. cut the heel down and rounded the toe in the 1950s because ropers asked for something they could stand up in all day. A shape that exists because of the job is the same argument the Woolrich and chore-coat pieces in the feed make about cloth. Unmarked's version is the wearable modern end of it, and sits closer to RRL territory than to novelty western.

items.title: A Closer Look at Bleu de Chauffe FW26
items.summary: The French workwear house's autumn bags in selvedge denim and stonewashed canvas, with the making shown.

_homepage.note: Bleu de Chauffe takes its name from the boiler-suit blue covered in the bleu de travail piece already in the feed, and it is one of the few makers still cutting and stitching canvas and vegetable-tanned leather by hand in the Aveyron. This drop puts selvedge denim on the bags rather than the trousers. Provenance-first rather than seasonal, which is the only reason a lookbook earns a slot here.

items.title: Woman badly injured in alleged attack in hospital ED
items.summary: ACEM's president calls ED violence hugely significant and hugely under-reported — the under-reporting is the story.

_homepage.note: A 73-year-old patient was allegedly assaulted inside the emergency department at Princess Alexandra. Peter Allely uses the case to press the college's line that occupational violence in EDs is systematically under-recorded nationwide, which is the part that reaches his own department rather than Brisbane's. It is the safety leg of the same problem as the regional workforce and ED-load stories already in the feed.

items.title: Jin Sakai returns in Ghost of Yotei: Most Wanted
items.summary: Sucker Punch's roguelike survival mode, with the Tsushima protagonist and all four stances, out 1 October.

_homepage.note: Most Wanted ships alongside the Echoes of Sekigahara narrative expansion in the Complete Edition, with a $14.99 upgrade if you already own the base game. This is the first-party post out of the September State of Play rather than the aggregated round-up already in the feed. The escalating-bounty structure makes it closer to an arcade mode than to the campaign, which is the part worth knowing before paying for the upgrade.

items.title: Enshrouded — 1.0 Release Date Reveal
items.summary: First-party confirmation that the survival game he has been playing in early access goes 1.0 on 15 October.

_homepage.note: Keen Games put PC and PS5 on the same day and pushed Xbox back to spring 2027 rather than ship it rough, which is the good version of that decision given he plays on both platforms it kept. This is the announcement post itself rather than coverage of it. It also sets up an odd month: Dragonwilds leaves early access on 15 September and Enshrouded follows on 15 October, so both survival games in the feed hit 1.0 inside thirty days.

items.title: Introducing Kosmo Foto's new film — Direktor
items.summary: Re-rolled Eastman Double-X in 35mm cassettes, sold in limited batches rather than as a standing stock.

_homepage.note: Double-X is the black-and-white cine stock behind Raging Bull and Oppenheimer, and getting it in a loaded 35mm cassette without hand-rolling bulk film is the actual news. Kosmo Foto is releasing it in limited batches, so it is not a shelf item — that matters if he wants any. It is the third strand of the same story as the Kodak range and China Lucky emulsion news already in the feed: new black-and-white stock is genuinely coming back.

items.title: Chabela Brings the Food of Mexico City to Thornbury
items.summary: A Thornbury dining room built by two people who spent five years eating in Coyoacán and could not find it here.

_homepage.note: Harry Lawrence and Karla Martinez opened on High Street after a decade of failing to find CDMX cooking in Melbourne, and the starters read as street snacks — prawn aguachile tostadas, corn poached in bone marrow — rather than a Tex-Mex menu. It is a short run up High Street from the Northcote and Preston places already in the feed. Worth keeping on the list for the nights when Nina and Community Wine House are booked out.

items.title: ECG Case 137 — The Monitor Says Extreme VT
items.summary: Three rhythm-strip features that tell you the monitor is screaming at an artefact, not a dying patient.

_homepage.note: A 55-year-old with exertional chest pain, and the monitor calls polymorphic VT — the discipline is in reading the strip rather than the alarm. The tells here are an onset with no R-on-T, a rate approaching 600bpm that no ventricle can sustain, and native QRS complexes marching through underneath at 60. ECG Case 130 is already in the feed; this one is the artefact counterpart to it, and the pulse-oximetry trace as a tiebreaker is worth carrying into the next resus bay.

items.title: Pressing Plants Warn Labels Off One Premium Vinyl
items.summary: The plants themselves are telling labels to stop ordering the coloured and splattered variants collectors pay a premium for.

_homepage.note: Straight from the manufacturing end: the additives that make a record look like a marbled sweet also make it noisier and less consistent than plain black, and the people running the presses have stopped being polite about it. With 297 records on the shelf, this is the difference between paying more for a worse object and knowing when the standard press is the audiophile choice. Sits neatly against the DMM-versus-lacquer piece already in the feed — both are about what actually reaches the groove.

items.title: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus — DR Congo
items.summary: The authoritative update on an outbreak now past 6,700 confirmed cases with a case fatality ratio near 48 per cent.

_homepage.note: DON616 has already run in the feed; this supersedes it with figures to 7 September, a 61st affected health zone in North Kivu, and the exported cases in Uganda and France. The detail that matters clinically is that Bundibugyo has no licensed vaccine or specific treatment — the Ervebo playbook does not apply here. For anyone who might one day take a febrile returned traveller's history, the geography and the numbers are the part worth holding.

items.title: Thee Sinseers Share Love Stories
items.summary: Joey Quiñones' East LA soul group land their second album on 18 September, and the label has posted the whole context.

_homepage.note: Thee Sinseers live one shelf across from Thee Sacred Souls, Menahan Street Band and the Daptone records already in the collection — same oldies lineage, same reverence for sweet harmony and warm brass. Quiñones has pulled this one toward earthier instrumentation, standup bass and guitars run hot through amps for a sixties-adjacent tone, and says it did not feel like making soul music at any point. First-party from Colemine, so the release detail and the pressing information are the real thing rather than a repost.

items.title: Mastering Persistent Air Leaks
items.summary: What to do with the chest drain that keeps bubbling, from conservative management through to ultra-protective ventilation.

_homepage.note: The pneumothorax that does not seal is a problem that starts in the ED and then becomes somebody else's, which is exactly why the far end of the algorithm is worth knowing before you refer. Weingart's crew walk the whole ladder — suction settings, blood patch, endobronchial valves, and eventually VV ECMO to let the lung rest. Pairs with the CCPU lung work: the same fistula you cannot see on a film is the one you have been hunting for with the probe.

items.title: Patient dies after referral 'forgotten' at Mildura hospital
items.summary: Up to 150 Victorian patients waited over a year because their paper referrals sat in a box, and Safer Care Victoria is now reviewing it.

_homepage.note: This is the Victorian health system he works inside failing at the least glamorous point — referral administration, on paper, in 2026. Mildura Base has been in the news all year for ED locum gaps and an executive restructure, and this is the consequence rather than the governance story. The state is mid-rollout of electronic medical records and CareSync Exchange; this is the argument for that rollout written in the bluntest possible terms.

items.title: Woolrich — History, Philosophy, Iconic Products
items.summary: The full account of America's oldest continuously operating outdoor clothing maker, mill and all.

_homepage.note: Woolrich is one of the four reference points the brief names, and until now the feed has had flannel, chore coats and Levi's dating guides but nothing on the mill itself. The through-line is worth having: railroad workers, two world wars, the buffalo check, and a woollen mill that never stopped running in Pennsylvania. It is the provenance argument for anything Woolrich-labelled you might find in a vintage rack on Smith Street.

items.title: Experimenting with IR Filters
items.summary: Side-by-side results from a stack of different IR filters, so you can see what each cutoff actually does before buying one.

_homepage.note: The Hi-Con IR piece in the feed covered the emulsion coming back; this is the other half of the problem, which is the glass in front of it. Comparative frames through several filters make the tradeoff legible — how far into the red you cut, how much exposure you give away, how strange the foliage goes. Practical rather than mystical, which is the useful register for a technique that mostly gets written about in adjectives.

items.title: First Look at the GTA VI Limited-Edition DualSense Controllers
items.summary: Two Vice City DualSense designs, with the pre-order date and the pricing, ahead of GTA VI's 19 November PS5 launch.

_homepage.note: First-party and dated, which is what makes it worth linking rather than the twenty aggregator rewrites of it — pre-orders opened 10 September, the controllers land 19 November alongside the game, and direct.playstation.com stock is limited. The white one is Vice City at daybreak, the black one is the nightlife; both are the usual haptics-and-adaptive-triggers pitch. If a GTA VI launch-day plan is happening, this is the bit with a deadline attached to it.

items.title: Can a Paediatric Emergency Department Fit Inside a Laptop?
items.summary: A hard look at the Victorian Virtual ED after 380,000 paediatric consultations — what it actually diverts, and what it does not.

_homepage.note: The VVED is a Victorian service, run out of Northern Health, and it is now one of the largest paediatric virtual EDs anywhere — so this is a piece about the department down the road from his, not a foreign model. Worth reading for what the data says about which presentations are genuinely safe to see through a screen and which quietly end up in a physical ED anyway. It is the system side of the same crowding story the regional-ED items in the feed were telling from the inside.

items.title: Bowness Photography Prize 2026
items.summary: Fifty finalists from 750 entries, hung at Wheelers Hill from today until 8 November.

_homepage.note: Australia's most significant photography prize, in its 21st year, and this year's field explicitly ranges across darkroom-based practice as well as digital — which is the part worth the drive out to Ferntree Gully Road. Judged by Natasha Bullock, Petrina Hicks and Anouska Phizacklea, with the winner announced on 17 September, so going after that date means seeing the field and the verdict together. It opens today and runs until 8 November, so there is no rush, but there is a reason to go.

items.title: Every Film Ever: An Interview with Lenny Alvarez
items.summary: The man cataloguing every film stock ever made, on why the boxes and the dead emulsions are worth keeping.

_homepage.note: A first appearance in the feed for Shoot It With Film, and a good reason for it — Alvarez is building the reference work nobody else is building, down to packaging for emulsions discontinued decades ago. Useful context for the Fomapan, Washi and China Lucky items that have run here recently: new stocks keep arriving, and almost all of them are reaching back to something that already existed. Read it as an argument for why the film you shoot has a history worth knowing.

items.title: Brunswick Picture House Is More Than Just a Movie Theatre
items.summary: The Thornbury Picture House pair's second cinema, in a converted 1920s petrol station on Sydney Road, where you can just come for a drink.

_homepage.note: Gus and Lou Berger took eighteen months over the conversion and built something bigger than Thornbury — eighty seats, a six-and-a-half-metre screen, and a bar that locals use whether or not anything is screening. The programming is the point: special screenings, DJ sets, live music, Q&As and independent festivals rather than a release schedule. Sydney Road Brunswick, so it is a tram ride rather than an expedition.

items.title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 6
items.summary: OCHA's running count on the Trishuli valley flood: over a thousand dead, thousands still unaccounted for, and the health system in the affected districts largely gone.

_homepage.note: The 26 August event is thought to have started with a glacier collapse on Langtang Lirung and ran 72km down the Trishuli, taking out 41 bridges along the way. What the sitrep documents is the second disaster — overcrowded camps, unsafe water, damaged health facilities and broken referral pathways — which is the phase where the casualty count stops being trauma and starts being communicable disease. A useful corrective to the way these events are reported once and then dropped.

items.title: SGEM#519: Pediatric Pulmonary Embolism and the PERC-Peds Rule
items.summary: A structured appraisal of the first big prospective attempt to rule out PE in children without radiating them.

_homepage.note: BEEPER is a multicentre prospective diagnostic-accuracy study of PERC-Peds, and the case it opens with — a 15-year-old with pleuritic chest pain after a viral illness — is the exact presentation where adult rules get applied to a paediatric body out of habit. Lauren Westafer is the guest skeptic, which is the right pairing: she researches PE diagnosis and implementation science, so the discussion goes past the numbers into whether a rule survives contact with a real department. Worth reading alongside the adult PE material already in the feed, because the failure mode here is the opposite one — under-testing a low-prevalence group.

items.title: Bowie's Young Americans, Half-Speed Mastered, Reassessed
items.summary: A cutting-room account of the Young Americans half-speed, and an argument that the 'plastic soul' record has been undersold.

_homepage.note: The technical detail is the point: 192kHz transfers of the original Record Plant masters, no additional processing, cut by John Webber at AIR on a recapped Neumann VMS80. Given how much Philadelphia soul sits in your collection — Sam & Dave, Solomon Burke, the Temptations — Bowie's attempt at the same idiom is worth hearing on a pressing that does not flatten it. Also a clean case study in what half-speed cutting actually buys you, which is the recurring argument on this site.

items.title: Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI
items.summary: A sober read on how much of the research-acceleration claim is real, from someone who annotates rather than amplifies.

_homepage.note: Willison's value here is that he sits between the announcement and the hype and quotes the specific claims being made about models doing original research. This is the same week the Navier-Stokes result was being passed around, and the interesting question is not whether a model can produce a proof but what the working process around it looked like. Relevant to anyone about to be told an AI tool will accelerate their department's evidence review.

items.title: PSOs to bolster security at Melbourne hospitals under proposal
items.summary: An election pledge to put armed protective services officers inside Melbourne hospitals, which would change who stands next to you at three in the morning.

_homepage.note: Occupational violence in EDs has been argued about in Victoria for a decade, mostly through code grey policy and duress alarms rather than uniformed officers on the floor. Putting PSOs — sworn, armed, and trained for railway stations — into a clinical environment raises the question of who de-escalates and who escalates, and that is a staff-safety debate with a live political deadline attached. Worth tracking because whatever wins the argument ends up in your department's response plan.

items.title: Exploring the Heritage of RRL
items.summary: The long version of where Double RL's vocabulary comes from, with the historians who actually hold the garments.

_homepage.note: RRL is one of the reference points the whole vintage-menswear interest hangs off, and this goes past the marketing into the sources: Lynn Downey on Levi's, Rin Tanaka and Larry McKaughan on the archives people buy from. Ralph Lauren founded it in 1993 off the Colorado ranch, and the piece is clear that the brand is a reading of real workwear, military utility and western clothing rather than an invention. Useful for knowing what you are looking at on a rack of old chore coats.

items.title: Episode 226: Superwarfarin Toxicity
items.summary: Recognition, reversal and the months of vitamin K that follow — the part of brodifacoum poisoning that outlasts the ED stay.

_homepage.note: Superwarfarins are the rodenticide that behaves nothing like warfarin: the half-life runs to weeks, so a normal INR at four hours means very little and the reversal decision is a different calculation entirely. Reandelar and Mitra keep it to the practical sequence — when to test, what to give, and how to set up the outpatient vitamin K course that actually prevents the bleed. It is the kind of low-frequency, high-consequence tox case that is worth having heard once before it walks in.

items.title: Washi W and Washi Y — Paper Roll Film, If You're Ready
items.summary: A working account of shooting emulsion coated on Japanese paper, including everything that goes wrong before it goes right.

_homepage.note: Washi's paper-base stocks are the far end of the emulsion experiments the feed has been tracking — the Fomapan ortho piece, the Lucky announcements, the Hi-Con IR revival. Paper base means no anti-halation layer, a transport that fights the camera, and development that behaves differently from anything on acetate, so the piece is mostly practical warnings. Good counterweight to the idea that new stock is just a new box.

items.title: Dragonwilds' price won't change at its 1.0 launch
items.summary: Jagex holds the price at $30 through the 15 September 1.0 launch, four days out.

_homepage.note: Worth noting against Enshrouded, which put its Steam price up by €10 on 8 September ahead of its own October 1.0 — two survival games you play, taking opposite approaches to leaving early access. Dragonwilds goes out on the 15th with the Scorned Wilderness raid closing the Kuldra saga, arrives on console the same day, and Jagex has committed to monthly updates after with a 2027 roadmap to come. If you were holding off on recommending it to anyone, the price question is settled.

items.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez Look Family History in the Eyes
items.summary: The story behind the record that lands on 25 September, told through a 1976 photograph of the brothers' father at Machu Picchu.

_homepage.note: Hermanos Gutiérrez are on your shelf, and this is the origin piece for the album rather than the press release — Alejandro bringing in charango and the Peruvian quijada, and the 70s salsa and cumbia records the brothers collect surfacing as organ parts. Dan Auerbach produces again at Easy Eye, so it is the third record in that partnership and the first to leave the American southwest behind. Two weeks out, which makes it the right time to read it.

items.title: Better Now Bakery Brings Vegan Treats to Brunswick East
items.summary: Lygon Street's first permanent home for a farmers'-market baker whose za'atar scrolls have a following already.

_homepage.note: Jai Johns did the Coburg, Carlton and Alphington market circuit for years before this shopfront, so the queue is inherited rather than built from scratch. The list is scrolls with dairy-free cheese and za'atar, Persian love cake with rosewater glaze and pistachios, and miso-caramel apple turnovers — plant-based without being an exercise in substitution. Brunswick East end of Lygon, which puts it in easy range.

items.title: Escape From Frida Crouton's Final Course in Northcote
items.summary: Three courses at Poke the Bear where the puzzles are hidden in the food, from the person who built Australia's first escape room.

_homepage.note: Owen Spear and Bec DiNapoli run it out of the Northcote cafe on Friday and Saturday nights, with the conceit that a dead chef's fortune gets divided according to what you solve. $139 a head in a group of three to eight, $159 for a pair, and the kitchen is doing actual food — a smashed beef burger on milk bun, tempura hoki tacos — rather than props. Filed under things worth the ten-minute drive when someone visits.

items.title: A Study in Deep Shade — A One Shot Story
items.summary: One frame, 8:30 on a hot English morning, and the whole reasoning behind it.

_homepage.note: The One Shot Story format is the closest thing 35mmc has to a masterclass: a single image, the conditions, and why the exposure was placed where it was. Deep shade in hard light is exactly the metering problem the slide-film piece in the feed dances around, so the two read well together. Short, and more useful than another camera review.

items.title: Awake in VF
items.summary: A resus case where the patient talks back mid-compressions, and the fix turns out to be a nerve block rather than another shock.

_homepage.note: Inferior OMI into refractory VF, CPR-induced consciousness, then a stellate ganglion block before successful PCI — three things that each derail a resus team's script in a different way. The teaching point that CPR-induced consciousness is not ROSC is the kind that only sticks once you have watched it happen. Pairs with the electrical-storm and cardiac-arrest ultrasound material already in the feed.

items.title: First listening impressions of the Hana EH MK II cartridge
items.summary: A $550 high-output moving coil that runs into an ordinary MM phono stage — the upgrade path for a 297-record collection without a new preamp.

_homepage.note: Hana's E Series MK II lands late September, and this is serial number 0001 before anyone else has heard one. The point of the EH over the EL is high output: it plugs into a moving-magnet input, so it sidesteps the step-up transformer or MC stage that usually gates the jump from moving magnet. Fine's read is that it keeps the quick, defined Hana signature while digging deeper in the bass than the price suggests.

items.title: Thee Sacred Souls x Victor Axelrod 45s
items.summary: Two songs from an album already on his shelf, rebuilt as reggae by Ticklah, with heavy dub versions on the B-sides.

_homepage.note: Thee Sacred Souls are in the library, and this takes "Waiting for the Right Time" and "One and the Same" from Got a Story to Tell and hands them to Victor Axelrod and The Inversions for a rocksteady rework. Axelrod is the arranger behind a lot of the Daptone house sound, so this is less a remix than a re-recording in a different idiom. Straight to the Daptone announcement rather than coverage of it.

items.title: Yarra council bans smart glasses from pools and playgrounds
items.summary: The council covering Fitzroy, Collingwood and Richmond has become the second in Australia to ban camera glasses from its pools, gyms and childcare centres.

_homepage.note: Yarra is also lobbying Canberra to temporarily ban importing smart glasses until privacy law catches up with wearables — a local council trying to legislate ahead of a consumer AI product. The trigger was Kmart's $89 Anko camera glasses going viral and selling out nationally, which is what moved this from a tech-conference problem to a Fitzroy Pool problem. Exemptions apply for people using them as a vision or hearing aid.

items.title: Nearly half of Victoria's roads in very poor condition
items.summary: The auditor-general puts a number on what every Victorian driver already suspects, and the maintenance shortfall is over $3 billion a year.

_homepage.note: 48% of the state road network now rates poor or very poor, up from 39% in 2021, with the very-poor share jumping from 26% to 37%. The audit found maintenance has shifted to reactive and safety-critical repairs only, and the gap between defects identified and defects fixed more than doubled between January 2025 and June 2026. Road surface quality is upstream of the trauma that arrives in an ED, which makes this less abstract than a typical infrastructure audit.

items.title: Red Wing renders the Blacksmith in chocolate roughout
items.summary: The Blacksmith in chocolate muleskinner roughout — a reverse-tanned leather that scuffs into character instead of out of it.

_homepage.note: The leather comes from S.B. Foot, the Minnesota tannery Red Wing has owned since 1987, which is why the boot can be talked about in terms of a specific hide rather than a colourway. Roughout is the flesh side out: it is the workwear answer to needing a boot that looks better dirty, and it sits with the moleskin and chore-coat material already in the feed. A drop rather than a trend piece, which is the only kind of fashion timeliness that matters here.

items.title: PS Plus confirms 10 new games for September 2026
items.summary: RuneScape: Dragonwilds hits the Extra catalogue day one on 15 September, so the 1.0 launch costs nothing if the subscription is already live.

_homepage.note: Dragonwilds leaving early access on 15 September has been in the feed, but the PS Plus Extra day-one detail is the part that changes the decision — the console version arrives at no extra cost rather than as a second purchase. It is RuneScape's first appearance on PlayStation, launching with the Scorned Wilderness raid and the Runite tier included. The rest of the September catalogue is listed alongside it.

items.title: Street Photography is Tough
items.summary: An honest account of why the genre defeats most people who try it, written by someone still failing at it rather than someone selling a workshop.

_homepage.note: Most street-photography writing is either a gear list or a Cartier-Bresson homily; this is the rarer kind that admits how much of it is standing around feeling conspicuous and coming home with nothing. Useful counterweight to the metering and technique pieces already in the feed, which handle the part of the problem that has an answer. Worth reading before the next roll gets loaded for a walk through Brunswick.

items.title: Marvel's Wolverine Review (PS5)
items.summary: Insomniac's verdict five days out, from the outlet that covers PlayStation properly rather than as one platform among four.

_homepage.note: The structural news is that this is linear rather than open world — a deliberate break from the Spider-Man and Horizon template, with combat built around a rage meter that trades control for damage. Push Square rate the face models and framerate as about the best the PS5 does in 2026. It lands 15 September, the same day Dragonwilds does, which makes for a crowded week.
