items.title: JC: To Protect and Serve…and Drop Off
items.summary: Philadelphia lets police drive stabbings and gunshot wounds straight to the trauma centre, and the outcome data is more awkward than the prehospital orthodoxy allows.

_homepage.note: Roughly 40% of penetrating trauma arriving at the author's hospital comes by police car, with PPD often halving the time an ambulance would take. It is the cleanest natural experiment going on scoop-and-run versus stay-and-play, and it lands differently from a Victorian ED where every penetrating trauma arrives via Ambulance Victoria with a full prehospital workup already done. Worth reading for what it says about how much of prehospital time is actually treatment.

items.title: Two new simple cameras are a positive sign for film's future
items.summary: Two established manufacturers deciding new film cameras are worth tooling up for is a better health indicator than any stock announcement.

_homepage.note: Lomography's reworked half-frame Simple Use Reloadable is the headline — a genuinely reloadable version of the disposable-shaped camera they first shipped in 2017. Bellamy's argument is that new-camera investment, not new emulsions, is the signal that matters, because it means a brand is betting on shooters who do not exist yet. Reads well against the half-framing and compact-camera-revival pieces already published.

items.title: Peter Gunn opens Shogunn yakitori pop-up in Collingwood
items.summary: A six-week, twelve-seat yakitori counter run single-handed by the chef behind Ides, in the room that used to be March.

_homepage.note: Gunn closed Ides and its bar March on Smith Street earlier this year; Shogunn is him alone behind a grill in the same dark room, doing a ten-dish $97 set. Skewers run chicken neck with nori, thigh and onion, skin with tobiko, meatballs with sansho, plus shokupan with pâté and miso-glazed eggplant off the bird. It is a limited run before he looks for a permanent site, so the window closes rather than the booking getting easier.

items.title: Ebola (Bundibugyo virus) — Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.summary: The primary-source count on an outbreak that has roughly doubled since the coverage you already read here.

_homepage.note: The ABC piece this feed carried in August was tracking case numbers; this is the WHO's own Disease Outbreak News, and as of 26 August it stands at 5,794 confirmed cases and 2,786 deaths — a 48.1% case fatality ratio across 60 health zones in six provinces, up from 54 zones a fortnight earlier. Bundibugyo is the Ebola species with no licensed vaccine and no specific treatment, which is why the spread rate reads differently to the 2018-20 Kivu outbreak. When numbers move this fast the source beats the reporting.

items.title: EM Quick Hits 73: Phenobarb, Bacteriuria, Vent Settings
items.summary: Four registrar-grade updates in one sitting, including the phenobarb-for-withdrawal question that keeps coming up on nights.

_homepage.note: Zoe Polsky's phenobarbital segment sits directly alongside the EMCrit IBCC alcohol-withdrawal chapter already in the feed — same drug, different house style, and worth hearing both arguments before you write the order. The asymptomatic bacteriuria piece is the other one to keep: 30-60% of nursing-home residents culture positive at baseline, which is the trap behind a lot of ED 'urosepsis' labels. Mike Weinstock's malpractice case, a 15-year-old with thunderclap headache after coughing sent home without imaging, costs five minutes and sticks.

items.title: Tasty Morsels 095: Blunt Cerebrovascular Injury
items.summary: The BCVI screening question compressed to something you can actually hold in your head during a trauma call.

_homepage.note: Blunt cerebrovascular injury is a classic fellowship-exam topic and a genuine miss in trauma — the Denver and Memphis criteria are easy to nod along to and hard to recall under pressure. The series is deliberately simplified for retention and built off Oh's Manual as its curriculum, which makes it better revision than a full review article. Emergency Medicine Ireland has never appeared in this feed and there are nearly a hundred of these in the back catalogue.

items.title: On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem
items.summary: An AI system apparently resolving a Millennium Prize problem, written up by someone who checks the claims before repeating them.

_homepage.note: OpenAI put an unreleased model on Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness and the agents landed a resolution roughly 88 hours after launch — a claim that is either a genuine step change or a category error, and Willison is careful about which. He is the right person to read here because he separates what has been verified from what has been announced. Pairs with the GPT-6 Astra post the feed carried last week for the full shape of what shifted this fortnight.

items.title: DMM or Lacquer? Which is Better?
items.summary: Why the mastering credit on a reissue jacket tells you something before the needle ever drops.

_homepage.note: Fremer had the same Wilco record cut both ways and reports the difference plainly: DMM sharper on transients and image edge definition, lacquer smoother and warmer through the midrange. That matters when you are choosing between pressings of something you already own, because a 180g reissue is not automatically the better object. Abbey Road and most cutting houses have since gone back to lacquer, which is itself most of the argument.

items.title: Depth of Field: The Art of the Unsharp Image
items.summary: Depth of field treated as a compositional decision first, with all the aperture arithmetic deliberately held back.

_homepage.note: Part one leaves out the maths entirely and asks what an out-of-focus zone is actually doing inside the frame — the more useful half if you already know how to stop down. Sroyon Mukherjee shoots pinhole through to phone, so it never collapses into a gear argument. Casual Photophile has not been in the feed since the Pentax PC35AF review, and its technique category is worth working through properly.

items.title: Melbourne Airport to open new pick-up and drop-off zones
items.summary: A concrete change to how you drop someone at Tullamarine, effective 6 October.

_homepage.note: The 56-year-old departures ramp closes and pick-up and drop-off shift to new zones, clearing ground for the international terminal expansion. It is small news that becomes annoying news if you learn it in the car at 5am with a flight to catch. Filed under news rather than melbourne because it is a Victorian infrastructure change, not somewhere to go.

items.title: The Men With Blue Jeans: Navy SEALs in Vietnam Wore Levi's
items.summary: Provenance writing at its best — why 501s ended up in the Mekong Delta, told by the men who wore them there.

_homepage.note: SEALs in late 1970 and early 1971 chose Levi's 501s and 505s over issued dungarees because denim drained faster, did not snag, and — the detail that earns the piece — was quieter when wet, which matters on a night operation. It is the same cloth-and-use logic running through the RRL and Woolrich end of the wardrobe, only sourced from primary interviews rather than a brand's own mythology. Reads as a companion to the vintage 501 collector's guide Heddels keeps alongside it.

items.title: Dragonwilds teases Scorned Wilderness and its Sept 15 raid
items.summary: What actually lands when Dragonwilds leaves early access on Monday, rather than just the fact that it does.

_homepage.note: The 1.0 drop is six days out and Scorned Wilderness is the headline: anima-torn floating islands, the Kuldra raid closing out the saga, and the Runite tier. The part worth reading is the combat pass underneath it — visceral attacks, wands and RuneScape's classic special attack bar, which changes how the game plays rather than just what is in it. You already have the Jagex launch announcement; this is the content detail sitting under it.

items.title: Preston Market Is Launching a New Night Festival Soon
items.summary: Preston Market stays open after dark for the first time, and it is this Friday.

_homepage.note: 6pm to 9pm on Friday 11 September, with Jessica Wilson of Fools, Latinx DJ collective Bellaqueo and Sri Lankan band Dynamics — a market you have only ever seen in daylight, run as an evening. It is a short ride up from Thornbury and the kind of one-off that is over before the monthly roundups catch it. First edition of a new thing, so it is worth seeing what it turns into.

items.title: How the compact film camera returned from the dead
items.summary: Where the new point-and-shoots actually are, as opposed to where the hype says they are.

_homepage.note: The Lomo MC-A and Pentax 17 have shipped; Analogue's aF-1 is still pre-order only and slipped again to Q3 2026, with lens manufacturing and the shutter mechanism named as the specific hard parts. That is useful if you have watched secondhand compact prices climb and assumed relief was coming — the new supply is slower than the coverage suggests. Stephen Dowling has run this since 2012 and reports the film trade rather than the camera market.

items.title: Walt Dickerson :: To My Queen
items.summary: Vibraphone approached from the opposite direction to the Milt Jackson already on your shelf.

_homepage.note: Your jazz corner runs through Milt Jackson on Soul Brothers/Soul Meeting and Oscar Peterson's Night Train — polished, swinging, sat right in the pocket. Dickerson plays the same instrument almost as a percussion device, with Andrew Hill on piano and Andrew Cyrille on drums, which makes To My Queen the obvious next thing if you want to hear what else a vibraphone can be. Aquarium Drunkard remains the most reliable source here for adjacent listening rather than reissue announcements.

items.title: Hundreds of regional doctors stop work over burnout and conditions
items.summary: The rolling Victorian public-hospital stoppages reached Grampians and Bendigo, ahead of a statewide 24-hour strike on 15 September.

_homepage.note: This is the first sustained industrial action by Victorian salaried doctors since 2002, and it is now working through the health services one at a time — inner-city hospitals in late August, Monash and Eastern, then Northern, Mercy and Austin. ASMOF is asking for 30 per cent over four years plus training and safety terms, so the outcome sets the conditions registrars work under for the next enterprise agreement. Free to read, unlike most of the coverage.

items.title: Celtic Guru: Van Morrison In The 80s — Beautiful Vision
items.summary: The opening instalment of a series that makes the case for Morrison's most dismissed decade as his deepest.

_homepage.note: You own Van Morrison, and almost certainly the canonical end of him rather than the stretch from Common One to Irish Heartbeat that this series works through. James Rooney reads Beautiful Vision as devotional repetition rather than a lapse in quality, which is a genuinely different way to hear those records. It runs album by album, so it is a listening project rather than a single read.

items.title: Analogue Productions announces UHQR editions of four Who albums
items.summary: My Generation, Tommy, Live at Leeds and Who's Next cut from the original tapes, with the mastering and pressing chain named.

_homepage.note: The Who are on your shelf, which makes this the rare reissue announcement worth reading rather than skipping. The detail is the point: original analog masters, lacquers by Chris Bellman at Bernie Grundman, pressed at QRP, with My Generation and Live at Leeds as 45rpm 2LPs and Tommy and Who's Next as 200g UHQRs. That is enough information to judge whether any of it beats what you already own.

items.title: Health-care AI is here. We don't know if it actually helps patients
items.summary: Ambient scribes and record-trawling risk flags are already in hospitals; almost none of it has been tested against patient outcomes.

_homepage.note: The tools described here — note-taking assistants, background models flagging patients from the record — are arriving in Australian EDs on procurement timelines, not evidence timelines. Given how hard you are made to argue for a change in practice from a randomised trial, the asymmetry is worth noticing before someone asks you to use one. Pairs badly, in a useful way, with the non-inferiority piece above.

items.title: You don't understand non-inferiority trials (and neither do I)
items.summary: Morgenstern takes apart the design that quietly underwrites half the trials you are asked to change practice on.

_homepage.note: Nearly every recent trial in this feed — ARISE-FLUIDS, RENOVATE, the ketamine-versus-etomidate RSI trial — hangs on a non-inferiority margin somebody chose before enrolment. This is the piece that explains why that choice does most of the work and why 'non-inferior' is not the same as 'equivalent'. Read once and it changes how you read journal club for good.

items.title: EMCrit Wee — 2026 PE Update F/u with Farkas & Morgenstern
items.summary: Farkas and Morgenstern argue out the disagreements the main PE update left hanging, which is where the useful thinking actually is.

_homepage.note: The feed already carries EMCrit 424, the PulmCrit hot take on PRAGUE-26 and First10EM on STRATIFY/STORM-PE — this is the conversation that ties them together, with two people who read the same trials and reached different bedside thresholds. Worth it for the reasoning about who actually gets catheter-directed therapy rather than the headline result. Short-format episode, so it is a commute rather than an evening.

items.title: How to Date and Value Vintage Levi's Type I, II and III Jackets
items.summary: The pocket, pleat and tab details that tell you what decade a jacket is from before you look at the price tag.

_homepage.note: This is the reference piece for reading a denim jacket in the wild — single pocket versus double, pleats, the red tab, the details that separate a 1950s Type II from a reproduction. Useful in exactly the places you actually shop, and it sits alongside the chore coat and bleu de travail histories already in the feed as the third leg of the workwear-outerwear canon. Old, and none the worse for it: the garments have not changed.

items.title: Enshrouded's final early access update revamps almost everything
items.summary: Forging the Path is the shape the game will actually launch in on 15 October, not a side patch.

_homepage.note: Keen rebuilt combat, weapon skills and animation behaviour in the last early access update rather than saving it for 1.0, so an old save will not feel like the game you left. The price also goes up today, 8 September, ahead of the October launch. Read it as the changelog for the version you will be playing rather than as news about a release date.

items.title: 0.12.1 and the Road to Release
items.summary: The last patch before 1.0 on 15 September: Agility as a full skill, a double jump, and the longest side quest yet.

_homepage.note: First-party notes rather than coverage of them, and the final content drop before Dragonwilds leaves early access next week. Agility arrives as a real skill tree with six timed courses, Kebbit Burrow shortcuts and an aerial dash, plus the Recall spell and The Great Body Robbery out of Bloodblight Swamp. Worth reading now so the 1.0 launch and the Scorned Wilderness raid land on a character that is already set up.

items.title: China Lucky Film announces two new black-and-white films
items.summary: A third and fourth new emulsion in twelve months from Lucky, which matters more than any single stock does.

_homepage.note: Lucky has now put out two colour films and is following with two black-and-white ones inside a year — that is a manufacturer scaling up, not a novelty run, and it is the counterweight to the Kodak price stories already in the feed. Details came via Reddit screengrabs on 6 September, so treat the specifics as provisional. Worth watching if you want a cheap B&W stock that is not Fomapan.

items.title: The OPTION Trial: Late-Window TNK for Non-LVO Stroke
items.summary: A CT-perfusion-selected thrombolysis result that widens who might get TNK at 4.5–24 hours, with the bleeding cost stated plainly.

_homepage.note: OPTION randomised CTP-selected non-LVO patients out to 24 hours from last-known-well: mRS 0–1 improved 34.2% to 43.6%, and symptomatic ICH went from 0% to 2.8%. That combination is exactly the conversation you end up having at 3am with a stroke team and a family, so it is worth having the numbers in your head rather than reaching for them. REBEL EM's appraisal is short on hype about the selection criteria, which is the part that will not travel to every ED.

items.title: Lemons and Lemonade — a Review of the Pentax PC35AF
items.summary: An honest account of a compact that keeps breaking and keeps getting fixed, and why people forgive it.

_homepage.note: Tocchio's verdict — 'horribly flawed, foolish to own... and yet, every time its shutter fires, unquestionably great' — is the most useful thing anyone writes about eighties point-and-shoots, which are now priced as if they were reliable. Fixed 35mm f/2.8, manual ISO to 400, manual advance: worth knowing what you would actually be buying before an op-shop find tempts you. Casual Photophile is new to this feed; the 35mmc well has been drawn on hard lately.

items.title: The Freehouse Opens in Collingwood With 24 Gluten-Free Drinks
items.summary: Twobays, the country's only fully gluten-free brewery, finally has a room of its own on Rokeby Street.

_homepage.note: A beer hall where all 15 taps and the other nine drinks are gluten-free is a genuinely useful address to have filed away for whoever in the group cannot drink normally — and the food is a Latin American menu from an ex-Vue de Monde and Stokehouse chef rather than an afterthought. Empanadas, adobo half-chicken, cast-iron provolone, crumbed whole snapper. 118 Rokeby Street, Wednesday to Sunday from 11.30am.

items.title: Melbourne's newest wine bar opened behind a roller door in Northcote
items.summary: Minimum Wines opened a small European-style bar at the back of their own Northcote winery — cheese, tinned fish, low-intervention pours.

_homepage.note: Matt and Leni Purbrick make the wine on site from their Goulburn Valley fruit and pour it through a roller door at the rear of the same building, which is about as short a supply chain as a Melbourne wine bar gets. Walking distance from the Northcote end of your usual run, and a different proposition from the Suze team's Nina pasta bar already in the feed. Small room, so it rewards going early.

items.title: WPW, tachy-arrhythmias and ischemic mimics
items.summary: Five real ECGs where pre-excitation is the trap — palpitations written off as anxiety, a pseudo-infarct pattern, and an MI hidden underneath the delta waves.

_homepage.note: Jesse McLaren's monthly ECG Cases is the closest thing going to a structured curriculum in occlusion-MI recognition, and the feed has been leaning on LITFL's ECG library for this until now. The last case here — infarction concealed by pre-excitation — is exactly the failure mode that survives a normal computer read. New source for the feed, and the strongest single ECG teaching series not yet in the pool.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra
items.summary: A working developer's first read on the new frontier model, with benchmark results treated as claims to be checked rather than announcements to be repeated.

_homepage.note: Willison is the useful counterweight to launch-day coverage: he runs the thing, reports what it actually does, and is explicit about which benchmark numbers he trusts. Worth ten minutes if only to calibrate how much of the current AI-in-medicine noise is downstream of models that materially changed in the last fortnight. Near-daily, so this is the source to check rather than the aggregators.

items.title: DRC's Ebola outbreak likely to become the worst in history: WHO
items.summary: The Bundibugyo-species outbreak in eastern DRC is spreading faster than any previous Ebola epidemic, and there is no licensed vaccine for this species.

_homepage.note: Bundibugyo is the detail that matters clinically: Ervebo covers Zaire ebolavirus, so the vaccine-and-ring-vaccination playbook from 2018–20 does not straightforwardly apply here. By early September WHO had it past 6,000 cases with most deaths still occurring in communities rather than treatment centres. Charted rather than narrated, which makes the trajectory legible in a couple of minutes.

items.title: Keeping the Flame Alive: Deep Funk Archival Compilations
items.summary: How Numero, Jazzman and BBE go about finding, licensing and sequencing the 45s that never got a second pressing.

_homepage.note: The shelf that holds Sharon Jones, Menahan Street Band, Thee Sacred Souls and the Solomon Burke sits directly next to this world — Daptone and Big Crown are the revivalists, these labels are the archaeologists who supplied the source material. The piece is good on the unglamorous part: chasing rights holders for records that sold three hundred copies in 1971. A map of where to dig next rather than a list of things to buy.

items.title: PulmCrit Hot Take: PRAGUE-26 on catheter-directed thrombolysis in PE
items.summary: A second multicentre RCT lands on catheter-directed lysis for intermediate-high risk PE, and Farkas reads it against HI-PEITHO rather than in isolation.

_homepage.note: The feed has already carried the 2026 Crashing PE update, the ANZ 'goodbye massive and submassive' reframing and the stratify-and-storm trial round-up; this is the trial that tells you whether any of that repositioning survives contact with a second RCT. Farkas's hot-take format is deliberately fast and provisional, which is the right register for a paper this new. Worth reading before the next intermediate-high risk PE lands in resus and someone asks whether to call interventional.

items.title: Victorian healthcare 'fundamentally broken', regional GP says
items.summary: AMA says five regional Victorian hospitals are showing signs of system failure, with GP shortage pushing primary-care presentations into EDs.

_homepage.note: This is the system story sitting underneath his waiting room: when regional primary care thins out, the overflow arrives at metropolitan and regional EDs as low-acuity volume that still has to be triaged, seen and dispositioned. The state's answer so far has been 29 urgent care clinics, and the ABC piece has the government's line next to the on-the-ground one. Free to read, unlike The Age's version.

items.title: Blowout: The Bell Bottom Tolls For Thee
items.summary: Shuck on the inverse-tapered leg — boot cut, flare, bell — as a construction problem of tight top block and open hem rather than a decade reference.

_homepage.note: Useful because it treats the flare as a pattern-making decision, which is how you tell a genuine 70s workwear cut from a costume version of one. That matters when sorting through vintage Banana Republic and Woolrich stock where the leg opening is the fastest way to date a pair. Heddels does most of the heavy lifting in this topic and this is the sort of piece that earns it.

items.title: Four reasons hyperangulated VL should be the ICU intubation mainstay
items.summary: An argument that the Mac blade is being asked to do a job it was never designed for, and that the hybrid technique most of us default to is the worst of both worlds.

_homepage.note: The core claim is about deliberate practice, not kit: if hyperangulated blade plus rigid stylet is your everyday technique, the obese, limited-mouth-opening patient at 3am is not a special case. It is the sort of piece that changes what you reach for on the next routine intubation rather than the next difficult one. Pairs directly with the airway end of CCPU-adjacent resuscitation work.

items.title: Fomapan FomaOrtho 400 – a film that might inspire you
items.summary: A user report on Foma's orthochromatic 400 stock, where red-blindness does something specific to skin and foliage rather than just looking vintage.

_homepage.note: Orthochromatic film is the cheapest way to change how a negative looks without changing a single piece of glass, and Foma's is the one that is actually stocked in Australia. Useful next to the slide-metering piece already in the feed: both are about deciding what a stock is for before loading it. Being able to develop under a red safelight is a side benefit rather than the point.

items.title: Now's the best time to get Enshrouded
items.summary: Keen Games is raising the price by €10 on 8 September, ahead of the 15 October 1.0 launch on PC and PS5.

items.title: Eastman Kodak's new range of films see UK price drop
items.summary: Wholesale cuts on Eastman Kodak's self-distributed stock are showing up as roughly 20% off at retail — the first real price movement in film in years.

_homepage.note: The Kodak self-distribution story has been building all year and this is the point where it reaches the shelf: Gold 200 in 35mm down £2 a roll, a five-pack of 120 down from £51 to £39.99. UK pricing is not Australian pricing, but the wholesale change is upstream of both, so it is a reasonable leading indicator for what Melbourne labs charge in a few months. New source for the feed and the one that covers stock and emulsion news properly.

items.title: The Suze Team To Open Nina, a Northcote Pasta Bar
items.summary: Giulia Giorgetti and Steve Harry are turning the old Vex Dining site on High Street into a pasta bar, opening this month.

_homepage.note: Their Fitzroy North wine bar Suze is barely eighteen months old, and Nina grows out of its Sunday pasta project — a menu written the morning it is served. 66–68 High Street puts it a short walk up from Northside territory, with about twenty wines by the glass drawn mostly from Italy and Australia. A single-venue Coming Soon piece rather than the monthly roundup, so it stays readable after the doors open.

items.title: POCUS Made Easy: CLUE Protocol
items.summary: The short cardiopulmonary look, for the shifts where a full RUSH is more scan than the patient has time for.

_homepage.note: CLUE pairs a basic echo with a lung exam and stops there, which is a different tool from the RUSH and I-RUSH protocols already sitting in the feed rather than a lesser version of them. For CCPU purposes it is a useful contrast case: same windows, deliberately narrower question, and a clear account of what you give up by not scanning further. Kimura's original 2011 paper is cited at the bottom if the derivation matters.

items.title: Melô do Embaixador: Brazilian Soul, Funk & Disco Covers
items.summary: Twenty-seven Brazilian readings of the soul and funk canon that takes up most of a shelf at home.

_homepage.note: The collection runs deep on the American originals here — James Brown, Curtis Mayfield, Parliament, Solomon Burke, and the Daptone descendants in Sharon Jones and Menahan Street Band. This is that same material passed through Brazilian studios between 1968 and 2015, sometimes translated into Portuguese, sometimes cut instrumental, sometimes sung in wonderfully approximate English. Tim Maia anchors it, but the anonymous studio bands and disco cash-ins are the reason to stay.

items.title: The Witcher 4 Finally Gets a Launch Window
items.summary: CD Projekt Red puts a year on the Ciri game, and it is further out than anyone was hoping.

_homepage.note: Nowakowski confirmed a 2028 target in a video posted ahead of Gamescom, and the game skipped the show entirely — no gameplay, no trailer. That reframes the Witcher 3 Remastered coverage already in the feed: the free remaster on 29 September and the Songs of the Past expansion in 2027 are now the whole Witcher plan for the next two years, not a warm-up act. Worth knowing before deciding whether to start another Blood and Wine run.

items.title: Hi-Con IR: Bringing Back True IR on Film
items.summary: Genuinely new emulsion rather than another house-branded respool of something that already exists.

_homepage.note: True infrared has been effectively gone from the film market since Kodak and Efke stopped making it, and most things sold as IR since are extended-red films that fake the look. This is the account of getting an actual IR-sensitive stock back into production — the coating problems, the handling constraints, why nobody else bothered. Emulsion news of the kind that is worth more than the tenth camera review of the month.

items.title: How I Meter Slide Film
items.summary: A working method for the one film stock where getting the exposure wrong costs you the frame outright.

_homepage.note: Omar Tibi's argument is that slide film asks you to invert the habit negative film teaches: protect the highlights, let the shadows fall. He shoots it without bracketing on cost grounds and explains how he gets away with that, which is the part most slide-film writing skips. Concrete enough to take out on the next roll rather than nod along to.

items.title: To squeeze or not to squeeze: the ARISE-FLUIDS trial
items.summary: A full appraisal of the one recent septic shock trial actually run in the departments he works in.

_homepage.note: ARISE-FLUIDS randomised early vasopressors against a larger fluid load in Australian, New Zealand and Irish emergency departments, so the case mix and the staffing are his, not an American ICU's. The feed already carries EMCrit 428, which passes over the trial in a roundup, and the 2026 Surviving Sepsis guidelines, which kept the 30 mL/kg suggestion anyway; this is the version that sits with the numbers long enough to say what the two arms actually received. Worth reading before the next time someone asks why the bag is still running.

items.title: ECG Case 130 — ECG Top 100 Self-Assessment Quiz
items.summary: A narrow-complex tachycardia in a well 25-year-old, and a notch in the inferior R waves explaining why she was ever going to get one.

_homepage.note: The Crochetage sign only exists for you if someone has pointed it out once: notching at the apex of the R wave in II, III and aVF, 92–100% specific for a secundum ASD when it appears in all three leads. Put it beside the RVH voltage and the incomplete RBBB and you have a structural diagnosis off a 12-lead in someone who looks entirely well. It sits directly against the ultrasound material already in the pool — this is the ECG that should make you reach for the probe.

items.title: Beyond The Tracks — How Railroading Impacted American Workwear
items.summary: Where the pocket placement, the stripe and the cut of every chore coat in the wardrobe actually came from.

_homepage.note: The feed already carries the chore coat, bleu de travail and flannel histories; this is the American railroad half of the same story, with companies ordering matched ensembles of cloth and print until uniformity for trainmen was standard practice by 1900. It is the origin of hickory stripe and of the silhouette RRL and Pendleton keep redrawing every few seasons. Read it as provenance for things already owned rather than as a shopping list.

items.title: Daptone Records Keeps Classic Soul and R&B Alive
items.summary: Four artists on your shelves record for this label, and the piece is about the tape machine they all pass through.

_homepage.note: Sharon Jones & The Dap-Kings, Menahan Street Band, Thee Sacred Souls and Jalen Ngonda are all Daptone or its imprints — a meaningful slice of the soul end of the collection running through one Brooklyn house band and one analogue chain. The twenty-five-year mark is the excuse; the substance is Gabe Roth and Neal Sugarman still refusing to leave tape while everything around them went to the grid. If you have ever wondered why those four records sound like siblings, this is the reason.

items.title: Transmissions: Sun Ra — Door of the Cosmos
items.summary: An hour that opens the far door of jazz without asking you to buy anything first.

_homepage.note: Night Train and the Milt Jackson–Ray Charles date are the collection's centre of gravity in jazz: swinging, tonal, comfortable. Sun Ra is the other edge of the same century, and a conversation with documentary director Drew DeNicola — plus rare Arkestra recordings and Moor Mother reading from The Immeasurable Equation — is a far gentler way in than starting on the discography cold. Aquarium Drunkard is already the deep-listening source in this feed; this is the episode to test that edge on.

items.title: Marvel's Wolverine: New Gameplay, Story Details From State of Play
items.summary: Insomniac's PS5 exclusive lands 15 September — the same day Dragonwilds leaves early access, so one of them waits.

_homepage.note: This is the State of Play showing with actual gameplay and story detail rather than the original teaser: Insomniac's first M-rated game, built only for PS5 with no cross-gen version. The 15 September date collides exactly with RuneScape: Dragonwilds 1.0, which is already in the feed — same day, same console, two very different games. Worth watching before deciding which one gets the fortnight.

items.title: Just a Sec
items.summary: The 1/focal-length rule was invented by somebody else's hands; this is how to find your own number.

_homepage.note: Geoff Chaplin takes the hand-held shutter-speed rule apart and tests the thing nobody bothers to test: the threshold is personal, and yours is probably not 1/50 on a 50mm. That matters far more on film than digital, where there is no stabilisation to hide behind and no chimping to tell you the frame was soft until the scans come back. It costs one roll to establish and then you stop guessing at the bottom end in low light.

items.title: EMCrit 427 — Advancing Concepts in Shock Physiology
items.summary: Two papers that reframe shock as four interfaces rather than one number, which changes what you do with the pressor.

_homepage.note: Rola, Kattan and Siuba's four-interface model splits resuscitation into macrocirculation, venous return, the microcirculation and the tissue itself, and argues each deserves its own target rather than a single MAP. This is the conceptual scaffolding underneath the RUSH exam already in the feed: the exam tells you which interface is broken, this tells you why that distinction matters at the bedside. Worth the hour if you want the CCPU physiology to hang together instead of sitting as a list of views.

items.title: Goodbye "Massive" and "Submassive"
items.summary: The two words you have used for every PE handover since medical school are gone; this is the short version of what replaced them.

_homepage.note: Nickson walks the new AHA/ACC A-to-E clinical categories and why "submassive" was too blunt to hold both the hypoxic patient who is sliding and the well one with a nudged troponin. This is the terminology half of the change that EMCrit's 2026 crashing PE update — already in the feed — handles on the management side. Category A going home from the department is the line that will surprise people.

items.title: Film Photography News — August 2026 Recap
items.summary: A month of film-stock news in one pass: what is actually being coated, and what you will be able to buy in six months.

_homepage.note: Analog.Cafe's monthly recaps track the supply side — coating lines, discontinuations, price moves — rather than camera launches, which is the half of the news that changes what goes in the fridge. Kodak's Ektacolor and Ektapan announcements and Harman's colour-negative experiments both landed this year, so the emulsion side is genuinely moving for the first time in a while. Read it for what to stock up on.

items.title: 50 Vinyl Pressings That Ruin the Streaming and CD Versions
items.summary: A buying list for the narrow case where a specific pressing genuinely beats the file, rather than another vinyl-is-warmer argument.

_homepage.note: The value is the specificity — named pressings, not formats in the abstract — which is the only question that matters once a catalogue title has been reissued five times and they all look the same on Discogs. With 297 records already in, most future additions are repeat pressings of things streaming already covers, so the mastering is the whole difference. Worth a scan before the next order.

items.title: EMCrit 428 — A Few Things: ARISE Fluids, Bicarb and More
items.summary: ARISE FLUIDS was run in Australian and New Zealand emergency departments, so its answer on early vasopressors lands in your resus bay rather than someone else's.

_homepage.note: The trial randomised a thousand patients across ANZ and Ireland and found restricted fluids with early vasopressors no better on days alive and out of hospital — which neither vindicates the 30 mL/kg mandate nor kills it. Weingart pairs the result with the bicarbonate literature in one sitting. Reads directly against the 2026 Surviving Sepsis guidelines episode already in the feed.

items.title: EMCrit 429 — RUSH 2.0: The I-RUSH and CRUSH Exams
items.summary: The RUSH exam re-cut as a standing hemodynamic map rather than a crash-only protocol — the version worth learning before the next CCPU sitting.

_homepage.note: Weingart's rebuild folds LVOT VTI and the interface model of hemodynamics into a scan you run on any undifferentiated hypotensive, not only the peri-arrest ones. That is the same territory CCPU examines, and it sits directly on top of the LITFL critical care ultrasound pages already in this feed. Better watched before your next shock case than after it.

items.title: "Half Framing" Practically Any Film Camera (Part 1 of 2)
items.summary: Turns half-frame into a technique you can run on a camera you already own instead of a second body you have to buy.

_homepage.note: The method needs nothing more than a double-exposure facility, which most of the usual suspects have, and it turns 36 exposures into 72 at a time when that arithmetic matters. 35mmc has twice earned a place in this feed on exactly this argument — use the camera you have, not the one you want. Part one is the method; the second half deals with what it does to scanning.

items.title: PlayStation State of Play September 2026: every reveal
items.summary: One page for everything Sony showed, and specifically for the dates that reorder a PS5 backlog.

_homepage.note: Final Fantasy Resonance took 22 October, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation went to April 2027, and Marvel's Wolverine was confirmed playable off a physical disc — a detail that carries weight given Sony is retiring PlayStation discs in 2028. Gran Turismo 7's Spec IV update splits across autumn and winter rather than landing at once. Skim it for dates, not trailers.

items.title: Jalen Ngonda on soul's timelessness and Doctrine of Love
items.summary: He is already on your shelf, and this is him explaining what he was reaching for on the record that follows.

_homepage.note: Doctrine of Love pushes past the orchestral sweep of the debut into horns and gospel-leaning backing vocals, with Chiarito and Buckley producing again for Daptone. The collection already holds Thee Sacred Souls, Sharon Jones & The Dap-Kings and Menahan Street Band, so this is that same house sound moving forward rather than an unfamiliar bet. The interview catches him mid-tour, talking about why sixties soul still holds.

items.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered: everything in the free upgrade
items.summary: A free upgrade to a game you almost certainly already own, with a date attached: 29 September.

_homepage.note: CD Projekt announced it at Gamescom for PC, PS5, Xbox Series and — natively for the first time — Switch 2, and anyone holding only the base game gets both expansions thrown in. PC Gamer's rundown is the one that lists what actually changed rather than replaying the trailer beats. Under four weeks out, so it is a decision about this month, not a wishlist item.

items.title: Banana Republic Archive Reissue Revives Safari Style
items.summary: Banana Republic has reissued its own safari-era archive — the exact thing you would otherwise be hunting secondhand.

_homepage.note: The Archive Reissue arrived with The Explorers Club and draws on the catalogue from the seventies through the early 2000s, which is the era vintage sellers have been pricing hard for years. Buying new is the cheap way to test whether those cuts actually work on you before chasing an original in the right size. Construction detail is thinner than Heddels would give you, but the reference points are the ones you already buy against.

items.title: Tochi Deli Reopens in Coburg, With the Same Great Sushi
items.summary: The Sydney Road sushi counter that vanished in July is trading again, ten minutes further north.

_homepage.note: Shingo and Rena Tochimoto ran the Brunswick market stall for five years before closing it; the Coburg room seats seventeen, sits across the mall from Half Moon, and carries the same nigiri, chirashi, donburi and onigiri at the same prices. Much of the fit-out is the old Brunswick timber unscrewed, sanded and reused. Northside, walkable from the 19, and cheap enough to be a weeknight rather than an occasion.

items.title: Higher risk PE management: STRATIFY and STORM-PE
items.summary: The two trials everyone is citing for intermediate-high-risk PE, read sceptically rather than reverentially.

_homepage.note: STORM-PE randomised only 100 patients and its primary outcome is RV/LV ratio at 48 hours — a surrogate, and Morgenstern says so plainly. STRATIFY's three-arm design (heparin alone versus catheter-directed versus systemic 20mg alteplase) is the one that matters for a department without an interventional service on site, which is most of them overnight. Worth reading before the guideline summaries harden into departmental policy.

items.title: EMCrit 424 – 2026 Crashing PE Update
items.summary: Weingart reconciles the AHA's A-to-E categories with the words you actually use at the bedside, then gives you an algorithm.

_homepage.note: The AHA's new alphabetic PE categories are the sort of thing that reads fine in a guideline and falls apart at 3am when the registrar has to say out loud what this patient is. This episode does the translation and then stratifies therapy across low-dose systemic lysis, mechanical thrombectomy, half-dose tenecteplase and ECMO, folding in STRATIFY and HI-PEITHO. Pair it with the First10EM appraisal of the same two trials, also in today's edition, and you have both the recommendation and the evidence behind it.

items.title: Research Roundup – June 2026
items.summary: A month of emergency medicine papers appraised in one sitting, with the weak ones named as weak.

_homepage.note: The monthly roundup is the cheapest way to stay current without reading journals, and it covers ground the podcasts skip — peripheral vasoactive administration among them, which is a live question in any department still moving pressors to a central line on principle. Skim the verdicts, read the two or three that touch your practice.

items.title: EMCrit 422 – SSC 2026 Sepsis Guidelines
items.summary: The lead author of the new Surviving Sepsis guidelines sits down and is asked which parts are actually bad.

_homepage.note: The 2026 rewrite carries 129 statements, 46 of them new ground, and it moves on things that change ED practice directly: high-flow nasal cannula as the first device in sepsis-associated respiratory failure, active fluid removal once resuscitation is done, and a recommendation against routine antipyretics. Having Hallie Prescott defend it live is more useful than reading the document, because the conditional recommendations are where the argument actually is.

items.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez Announce 'Los Ojos del Cóndor'
items.summary: The third Auerbach-produced record from a duo already on your shelf, out 25 September and worth a pre-order.

_homepage.note: Hermanos Gutiérrez are in the library, so this is a record to have on order rather than discover late. The pitch is a move off the American desert and into the Andes — Peru, their great-grandfather's country — which is a real change of vocabulary from El Bueno y el Malo and Sonido Cósmico rather than a third go at the same reverb. items.title: The Next Ascent
items.summary: What to work on once you can already expose correctly and the pictures still are not good.

_homepage.note: This is the plateau piece — written for the point where the mechanics are automatic and the limiting factor has become how you read light rather than what your meter says. The specific argument is about midtones and restraint, and about testing a stock properly instead of collecting stocks, which is a more useful discipline than another camera. Sits directly against the 35mmc one-camera piece already in your feed.

items.title: Eastman Kodak Goes Big and Shows Film Some More Love
items.summary: Tri-X 400 in 100-foot bulk rolls is back, which is the cheapest your black and white will ever get per frame.

_homepage.note: The headline is large format, but the line that matters for a 35mm shooter is the return of 100-foot bulk rolls of Tri-X 400 and Ektapan. Bulk loading is the one lever left on film cost now that per-roll prices have settled where they have, and this is the first time the newly in-house Eastman Kodak range has offered it. It also effectively closes out Kodak's move to take distribution back from Alaris, fourteen years on.

items.title: Internet Fashion Label Mutimer's Collingwood Store Opens
items.summary: Six years direct-to-consumer, and now there is finally somewhere in Melbourne to try the fit on.

_homepage.note: 308 Smith Street, so a tram ride rather than a postal gamble on sizing — which for a label you have only ever bought online is the whole point. Worth a walk down from Collingwood on a Saturday, and the closest thing Melbourne has to a home store for the label.

items.title: All About Flannel – Winter Fabric from Wales
items.summary: Why the word once meant wool, and how to tell a real flannel from a plaid-printed cotton shirt.

_homepage.note: Flannel is a nap and a finish, not a check — the pattern is the thing everyone mistakes for the cloth. The Welsh origin and the Pendleton century that followed are the useful part here, because Pendleton and Woolrich are the reference points you buy against, and both still trade on a wool flannel most of the market has quietly swapped for brushed cotton. Good reading going into a Melbourne spring, when the vintage racks fill with last winter's shirts.
